chunks.text: INSURANCE REGULATORY AND DEVELOPMENT AUTHORITY ACT, 1999 ENACTED: December 1999 COMMENCED: April 19, 2000 OBJECTIVE: Establish regulatory authority for insurance sector ESTABLISHMENT OF IRDAI: SECTION 3 - ESTABLISHMENT: Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) established as statutory body. COMPOSITION: - Chairperson (appointed by Central Government) - 10 Members: * 5 full-time members * 4 part-time members (Government nominees) * 1 member from SEBI HEADQUARTERS: Hyderabad FUNCTIONS OF IRDAI (Section 14): 1. REGULATORY FUNCTIONS: ✓ Issue licenses to insurers, intermediaries ✓ Renew, suspend, cancel licenses ✓ Regulate premium rates ✓ Regulate investment of funds ✓ Regulate maintenance of solvency margins ✓ Regulate insurance agents training 2. DEVELOPMENTAL FUNCTIONS: ✓ Promote growth of insurance industry ✓ Encourage insurance penetration ✓ Protect policyholders' interests ✓ Establish grievance redressal machinery ✓ Promote professional organizations 3. MONITORING FUNCTIONS: ✓ Conduct inspections and audits ✓ Monitor solvency margins ✓ Call for information from insurers ✓ Investigate complaints ✓ Take corrective action POWERS OF IRDAI: A. LICENSING POWER: - Grant insurance business licenses - Specify conditions for licenses - Suspend/cancel licenses for violations B. REGULATORY POWER: - Issue regulations and guidelines - Specify terms and conditions of policies - Regulate commission structures - Set standards for intermediaries C. INVESTIGATION POWER: - Inquire into insurer's affairs - Inspect books and records - Summon persons for examination - Punish for contempt D. ADJUDICATION POWER: - Impose penalties (up to Rs. 25 lakhs per violation) - Directions for rectification - Compensation orders KEY REGULATIONS ISSUED BY IRDAI: 1. Protection of Policyholders' Interests Regulations, 2017 2. Insurance Advertisements and Disclosure Regulations, 2021 3. Corporate Governance Guidelines, 2016 4. Insurance Brokers Regulations, 2018 5. Insurance Surveyors and Loss Assessors Regulations, 2015 6. Obligations to Rural/Social Sectors Regulations 7. Minimum Information Memorandum Regulations 8. Appointed Actuary Regulations 9. Investment Regulations 10. Solvency Margin Regulations POLICYHOLDER PROTECTION MEASURES: 1. INSURANCE OMBUDSMAN: - Free grievance redressal - Awards up to Rs. 1 crore (from 2024) - 17 ombudsman centers across India - Binding on insurers 2. GRIEVANCE REDRESSAL CELL: - Within IRDAI - Escalation point - Can direct insurers 3. INTEGRATED GRIEVANCE MANAGEMENT SYSTEM (IGMS): - Online complaint portal - Track complaint status - Time-bound resolution 4. MANDATORY DISCLOSURES: - Policy documents in simple language - Claim settlement ratios published - Financial strength ratings - Complaint statistics CLAIM SETTLEMENT MONITORING: IRDAI mandates: ✓ Settlement within 30 days ✓ Repudiation with clear reasons ✓ Quarterly reporting of claim ratios ✓ Public disclosure of statistics ✓ Penalties for delays INDUSTRY NORMS PRESCRIBED: 1. SOLVENCY MARGINS: - Life: 150% of required margin - General: 150% of required margin - Health: 150% of required margin 2. INVESTMENT PATTERN: - % in government securities - % in approved securities - Exposure limits 3. EXPENSE MANAGEMENT: - Caps on expenses of management - Commission limits - Administrative cost controls 4. RURAL/SOCIAL SECTOR OBLIGATIONS: - 7 lives per agent in rural areas - Specified percentage of premium from rural - Social sector coverage mandates PENALTIES UNDER IRDAI ACT: Violation |

Penalty ----------|-------- License conditions breach | Up to Rs. 25 lakhs Failure to furnish information | Rs. 5 lakhs Continued violation | Rs. 5,000 per day Obstruction of inspection | Imprisonment + fine False information | Rs. 10 lakhs APPELLATE MECHANISM: IRDAI Order → SAT (Securities Appellate Tribunal) → High Court → Supreme Court FDI IN INSURANCE: Historical Changes: - 2000: 26% FDI allowed - 2015: Increased to 49% - 2021: Increased to 74% (under approval route) COMPOSITE LICENSE: - Separate licenses for Life and General insurance - No cross-holding allowed - Exception: Reinsurers can hold composite license (from 2021) HEALTH INSURANCE: - Initially part of general insurance - Standalone health insurers allowed from 2006 - Specialized regulations for health insurance - Cashless network mandates MICRO INSURANCE: - IRDAI (Micro Insurance) Regulations, 2015 - Low premium products - Simplified underwriting - Rural penetration focus - Agent commission structure specified BANCASSURANCE: - Banks can act as corporate agents - Tie-ups regulated - Mis-selling prevention norms - Commission structures prescribed IRDAI ACHIEVEMENTS: ✓ Insurance penetration increased from 2.7% (2000) to 4.2% (2024) ✓ Life insurance density improved significantly ✓ Health insurance growth (post-COVID surge) ✓ Claim settlement ratios improved (95%+ in many companies) ✓ Consumer awareness enhanced ✓ Digital insurance ecosystem promoted RECENT INITIATIVES: ✓ Sandhi (Online dispute resolution) - 2024 ✓ Bima Bharosa (Integrated complaint portal) ✓ Use & File procedures (faster product approvals) ✓ Risk-based capital norms (under implementation) ✓ Digital KYC for instant policy issuance ✓ Elimination of medical tests up to certain sum insured CHALLENGES: ✗ Insurance penetration still low vs developed countries ✗ Rural reach insufficient ✗ Claim rejection rates (though improving) ✗ Mis-selling by agents (being addressed) ✗ Product complexity (being simplified) FUTURE ROADMAP: ✓ Insurance-for-all by 2047 ✓ Increased rural penetration ✓ Simplified product structures ✓ Enhanced digital distribution ✓ Mandatory insurance for certain segments ✓ Integration with Ayushman Bharat and other schemes CONTACT IRDAI: Address: Sy No. 115/1, Financial District, Nanakramguda, Gachibowli, Hyderabad - 500032 Phone: 040-20204000 Toll-Free: 155255 (or) 1800 4254 732 Email: complaints@irdai.gov.in Website: www.irdai.gov.in Integrated Grievance Management System (IGMS): https://igms.irda.gov.in/ Source: IRDAI Act, 1999 + IRDAI Regulations

= Service under Consumer Protection Act - Claim rejection challengeable as deficiency - Wrongful repudiation = unfair trade practice - Compensation for mental agony available - Consumer forums have jurisdiction ENFORCEMENT: Violations enforced through: 1. IRDAI penalties 2. License cancellation 3. Criminal prosecution 4. Policyholder complaints 5. Judicial review RECENT TRENDS: ✓ Digital policy issuance ✓ Instant claims settlement (health insurance) ✓ Standardization of policy wordings ✓ Elimination of medical tests for certain limits ✓ Cashless everywhere (health insurance) ✓ Video-based KYC ✓ Elimination of renewal documentation CHALLENGES: ✗ Low insurance penetration in India (~4% of GDP) ✗ High claim rejection rates (improving) ✗ Complex policy wordings (being simplified) ✗ Mis-selling by agents (being addressed) Source: Insurance Act, 1938 + IRDAI Act, 1999 Bare Act available at: indiacode.nic.in

INSURANCE ACT, 1938 - KEY PROVISIONS SUMMARY ENACTED: 1938 LAST MAJOR AMENDMENT: 2015 ADMINISTERED BY: Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) OBJECTIVE: Regulate insurance business in India and protect policyholders' interests PART I - PRELIMINARY (Sections 1-2) SECTION 2 - DEFINITIONS: - Insurance business - Life insurance - General insurance - Insurer, insured, policyholder - Premium, policy, sum insured PART II - BUSINESS OF INSURANCE (Sections 3-16) SECTION 3 - PROHIBITION OF INSURANCE BUSINESS: - No person shall carry on insurance business in India unless: * Registered under Companies Act * Holds certificate from IRDAI - Penalty: Imprisonment up to 3 years + fine SECTION 5 - DEPOSIT WITH CENTRAL GOVERNMENT: - Life insurer: Rs. 5 crores - General insurer: Rs. 10 crores SECTION 6 - CAPITAL REQUIREMENTS: - Minimum paid-up capital: * Life insurance: Rs. 100 crores * General insurance: Rs. 100 crores * Reinsurance: Rs. 200 crores SECTION 10 - SHARE TRANSFER RESTRICTIONS: - Prior approval required for transfer of shares exceeding 5% SECTION 11 - CHANGE IN MANAGEMENT: - Prior approval from IRDAI required for: * Appointment/removal of CEO, MD, Directors * Change in shareholding pattern SECTION 14 - POLICY TO SPECIFY MATTERS: Insurance policy must clearly state: - Names of parties - Premium amount and payment terms - Sum insured - Events covered/excluded - Terms and conditions - Nomination facility PART III - MANAGEMENT (Sections 17-29) SECTION 17 - BOARD OF DIRECTORS: - At least 50% directors with professional experience - Independent directors (as per Companies Act) SECTION 27A - CHIEF EXECUTIVE OFFICER: - Appointment, removal, remuneration subject to IRDAI approval PART IV - INVESTMENTS (Sections 27AA-29) SECTION 27A: INVESTMENT REGULATIONS: - Minimum % in approved securities: * Government securities * Government guaranteed bonds * Infrastructure bonds - Maximum exposure limits per investee SECTION 27B: MAINTENANCE OF ASSETS: - Adequate assets to meet liabilities - Solvency margin requirements PART V - MISCELLANEOUS PROVISIONS (Sections 30-114) SECTION 38 - ASSIGNMENT AND NOMINATION: - Policyholder can assign policy rights - Nomination facility in life insurance - Assignment takes precedence over nomination SECTION 39 - NOMINATION: - Life insurance only - Can nominate one or more persons - Nomination can be changed anytime - Nominee rights vs legal heirs rights SECTION 40 - LIMIT ON INSURANCE PREMIUM: - Payment through cash limited to Rs. 50,000 - Higher premiums via cheque/electronic mode only SECTION 41 - PROHIBITION OF INDUCEMENT: - No person shall offer rebate/incentive beyond policy terms - Penalty: Rs. 10 lakhs + cancellation of license SECTION 42 - COMMENCEMENT OF RISK: - Risk commences from date of policy issuance - Premium must be paid before commencement SECTION 45 - POLICY NOT TO BE CALLED IN QUESTION: MOST IMPORTANT PROVISION FOR POLICYHOLDERS "No policy of life insurance shall be called in question on any ground whatsoever after the expiry of three years from: (a) the date of the policy, or (b) the date of commencement of risk, or (c) the date of revival of the policy, or

(d) the date of the rider, whichever is later" KEY POINTS: - Policy becomes incontestable after 3 years - Insurer cannot reject claim on ground of non-disclosure - Exceptions: Fraud proven with clear evidence - Burden of proving fraud on insurer SECTION 47 - INSURABLE INTEREST: Life Insurance: - Insurable interest required at inception - Not required at claim stage General Insurance: - Insurable interest required at inception and claim stage SECTION 54 - INSURER TO FURNISH INFORMATION: - Policyholders entitled to policy documents - Information about premium allocation - Fund performance (in ULIP/investment plans) SECTION 64VB - INSURANCE OMBUDSMAN: - Free grievance redressal mechanism - Awards up to Rs. 50 lakhs (now Rs. 1 crore from 2024) - Binding on insurer (not on policyholder) SECTION 64UM - CLAIM SETTLEMENT: - Claims must be settled/repudiated within 30 days - Delay requires intimation to policyholder with reasons - Interest payable on delayed settlements SECTION 101 - CONTROLLER OF INSURANCE ACCOUNT: - Government appoints Controller - Oversees accounts and financial health SECTION 102 - RETURNS: - Annual returns to IRDAI - Balance sheet, profit & loss account - Actuarial reports SECTION 110 - PENALTIES: - Violation of Act: Up to Rs. 10 lakhs - Repeat violation: Cancellation of license - Imprisonment for major violations SECTION 110A - WINDING UP: - Only court can wind up insurance company - Policyholders' interests protected first KEY AMENDMENTS: 2015 AMENDMENT: ✓ Increased FDI limit to 49% (now 74% from 2021) ✓ Raised capital requirements ✓ Strengthened Section 45 (3-year incontestability) ✓ Enhanced Section 64UM (claim timeline) 2021 INSURANCE ACT AMENDMENT: ✓ FDI limit increased to 74% ✓ Composite license for reinsurers ✓ Surrender value regulations strengthened IRDAI ACT, 1999 - COMPLEMENTARY: Created Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority with powers to: - License insurers - Regulate premium rates - Protect policyholders - Promote insurance sector growth - Conduct inquiries and inspections KEY IRDAI REGULATIONS: ✓ Protection of Policyholders' Interests Regulations ✓ Insurance Advertisements and Disclosure Regulations ✓ Obligations of Insurers to Rural and Social Sectors ✓ Corporate Governance Guidelines ✓ Appointed Actuary Regulations ✓ Insurance Brokers Regulations ✓ Survey and Loss Assessors Regulations CONSUMER PROTECTION INTERFACE: Insurance = Service under Consumer Protection Act - Claim rejection challengeable as deficiency - Wrongful repudiation = unfair trade practice - Compensation for mental agony available - Consumer forums have jurisdiction ENFORCEMENT: Violations enforced through: 1. IRDAI penalties 2. License cancellation 3. Criminal prosecution 4. Policyholder complaints 5. Judicial review RECENT TRENDS: ✓ Digital policy issuance ✓ Instant claims settlement (health insurance) ✓ Standardization of policy wordings ✓ Elimination of medical tests for certain limits ✓ Cashless everywhere (health insurance) ✓ Video-based KYC ✓ Elimination of renewal documentation CHALLENGES: ✗ Low insurance penetration in India (~4% of GDP) ✗ High claim rejection rates (improving) ✗ Complex policy wordings (being simplified) ✗ Mis-selling by agents (being addressed) Source: Insurance Act, 1938 + IRDAI Act, 1999 Bare Act available at: indiacode.nic.in

SECTION 18 - RERA ACT, 2016 RETURN OF AMOUNT AND COMPENSATION (Detailed Analysis) STATUTORY TEXT: "18. (1) If the promoter fails to complete or is unable to give possession of an apartment, plot or building,— (a) in accordance with the terms of the agreement for sale or, as the case may be, duly completed by the date specified therein; or (b) due to discontinuance of his business as a developer on account of suspension or revocation of the registration under this Act or for any other reason, he shall be liable on demand to the allottee, in case the allottee wishes to withdraw from the project, without prejudice to any other remedy available, to return the amount received by him in respect of that apartment, plot, building, as the case may be, with interest at such rate as may be prescribed in this behalf including compensation in the manner as provided under this Act: Provided that where an allottee does not intend to withdraw from the project, he shall be paid, by the promoter, interest for every month of delay, till the handing over of the possession, at such rate as may be prescribed." ANALYSIS: 1. TRIGGER CONDITIONS: Two situations trigger Section 18: (a) Failure to give possession as per agreement terms/date (b) Discontinuance of business due to registration revocation 2. TWO OPTIONS FOR ALLOTTEE: OPTION A: WITHDRAW FROM PROJECT - Claim full refund of amount paid - Plus interest at prescribed rate - Plus compensation for losses - Terminates agreement - No further obligations OPTION B: CONTINUE WITH PROJECT - Don't withdraw - Claim interest for delay period - Interest till possession given - Agreement continues - Right to possession maintained 3. INTEREST RATE: "at such rate as may be prescribed" means: - State government prescribes rate in rules - Typically: SBI MCLR + 2% per annum - Example rates (2024): * Maharashtra: MCLR + 2% = 10.85% * Karnataka: MCLR + 2% = 10.85% * UP: MCLR + 1% = 9.85% 4. CALCULATION OF DELAY: START DATE: Due date of possession as per agreement - Include grace period if mentioned - Plus force majeure exclusions (if proved) END DATE: - If withdrawn: Date of refund order - If continuing: Date of actual possession 5. INTEREST CALCULATION: Simple Interest formula: (Principal Amount × Rate × Time Period in years) / 100 On which amount: - All amounts paid including: * Booking amount * Installments * Stamp duty (if paid) * Registration charges (if paid) * Any other charges collected 6. "WITHOUT PREJUDICE TO ANY OTHER REMEDY": Means allottee can also: - File consumer complaint - Claim damages - Seek specific performance - Criminal complaint (if fraud) - Civil suit SECTION 18 does not bar other remedies. 7. COMPENSATION: Under Section 18, compensation includes: - Actual financial loss - Rent paid due to delayed possession - Increased property prices (opportunity loss) - Mental agony (as per consumer law precedents) Claimed separately under Sections 71-72 before Adjudicating Officer. 8. ENFORCEMENT: If

promoter doesn't comply: - Recovery as arrears of land revenue - Attachment of property - Prosecution under Section 69 - Penalty under Section 63 (5% of project cost) - Imprisonment up to 3 years 9. LIMITATION: No specific limitation prescribed in Act. Generally complaints filed within 3 years from: - Date of possession default, OR - Knowledge of default 10. APPELLATE REMEDY: RERA Order → Appellate Tribunal (60 days) → High Court (60 days) KEY JUDICIAL INTERPRETATIONS: 1. NEWTECH PROMOTERS vs STATE OF UP (2021 SCC): - Section 18 is retrospective - Applies to agreements pre-RERA - Ongoing projects bound - Contractual terms don't override RERA - Interest rate as per RERA, not agreement 2. IMPERIA STRUCTURES vs ANIL PATNI (2020): - Unqualified right to withdraw or stay - Not dependent on contingencies - Extension of time doesn't affect interest liability - "Without prejudice" means cumulative remedies 3. FORTUNE INFRASTRUCTURE vs TREVOR D'LIMA (2018): - Definite timelines required - "Expected date" not acceptable - Buyer can't be made to wait indefinitely 4. PIONEER URBAN vs GOVINDAN RAGHAVAN (2019): - Reasonable interest rate = State Bank rate - Dominant agreements terms can't override - Builder-buyer parity in interest rates SECTION 19(4) - SYMMETRY: "The promoter shall be liable to pay such interest for every month of delay, till the handing over of the possession, which shall be at the same rate as the promoter shall be liable to the allottee, in case of default." Meaning: Same interest rate applies to: - Promoter's delay in giving possession - Allottee's delay in paying installments PRACTICAL APPLICATION: Scenario 1: WITHDRAWAL - Agreement date: 2020 - Due possession: 2022 - Amount paid: Rs. 50 lakhs - Delay: 2 years - Interest @ 10.85%: Rs. 10.85 lakhs - Total refund: Rs. 60.85 lakhs Scenario 2: CONTINUE - Same facts - Plus possession given in 2024 - Interest for 2 years: Rs. 10.85 lakhs - Buyer takes possession - Pays balance (if any) DEFENSES PROMOTERS CANNOT USE: ✗ Force majeure (unless proven with evidence) ✗ "Expected date" was tentative ✗ Regulatory delays (unless beyond control) ✗ Buyer delayed some payments (unless substantial) ✗ Agreement says "no interest payable" ✗ Extension granted by authority DEFENSES THAT MAY WORK: ✓ Actual force majeure (war, natural disaster - proven) ✓ Court/NCLT stay orders (with certified copies) ✓ Buyer defaulted substantially in payments ✓ Possession offered but buyer didn't take ✓ Authority/court granted timeline extension DOCUMENTATION FOR CLAIM: 1. Registered agreement copy 2. All payment receipts 3. Demand letters from promoter 4. Correspondence (emails, letters) 5. Project registration certificate 6. Advertisement/brochure 7. Possession notice (if any) 8. Bank statements TIMELINE FOR RESOLUTION: RERA Authority: 60 days (as per Rules) Appellate Tribunal: 60 days High Court: Varies (6 months to 2 years) COSTS: Filing fee: Nominal (Rs. 1,000 - 5,000) Advocate fee: Rs. 25,000 - Rs. 1,00,000 If successful: Recoverable from promoter CONCLUSION: Section 18 is the MOST POWERFUL provision for homebuyers. Creates absolute liability on promoter for delayed possession. Interest compensates
for time value of money. Choice given to buyer - withdraw or continue. Easy enforcement mechanism. Source: RERA Act 2016 + Supreme Court Judgments

MAHARASHTRA REAL ESTATE (REGULATION AND DEVELOPMENT) RULES, 2017 NOTIFICATION: December 6, 2016 (Effective from May 1, 2017) AUTHORITY: Maharashtra Real Estate Regulatory Authority (MahaRERA) WEBSITE: https://maharera.mahaonline.gov.in/ PART I - PRELIMINARY (Rules 1-2) RULE 1 - SHORT TITLE & COMMENCEMENT: - Maharashtra RERA Rules, 2017 - Came into force on May 1, 2017 RULE 2 - DEFINITIONS: - Act means RERA Act, 2016 - Authority means MahaRERA - Form means forms in Schedule - Carpet area, promoter, allottee as per Act PART II - REGISTRATION OF PROJECTS (Rules 3-10) RULE 3 - FORM FOR REGISTRATION: - Promoter to apply in Form 'A' - Online submission at MahaRERA portal - Fees: 0.5% of estimated project cost (min Rs. 1 lakh, max Rs. 10 lakhs) RULE 4 - DOCUMENTS TO BE SUBMITTED: - Land title documents - Commencement certificate - Approved building plans - Proforma of allotment letter - Proforma of agreement for sale - Encumbrance certificate - List of ongoing litigation RULE 5 - SCRUTINY AND REGISTRATION: - Authority scrutinizes within 30 days - Can seek additional information - Issues registration certificate with unique number - Valid till completion certificate obtained RULE 6 - DISPLAY OF REGISTRATION: - Registration number on all advertisements - On website, project site, marketing materials - Font size and prominence specified RULE 7 - QUARTERLY PROGRESS REPORT: - Promoter submits every quarter - Physical progress vs financial progress - Certified by architect/engineer - Non-compliance = penalty RULE 8 - PROJECT WEBSITE: - Mandatory project-specific website - Details of approvals, plans, completion timeline - Contact information - Updated quarterly RULE 9 - EXTENSION OF REGISTRATION: - Application 3 months before expiry - Reasons for delay - Revised timeline - Authority may grant extension RULE 10 - REVOCATION OF REGISTRATION: - For violation of Act/Rules - Show cause notice before revocation - Opportunity of hearing - Appeal to Appellate Tribunal PART III - REGISTRATION OF AGENTS (Rules 11-14) RULE 11 - APPLICATION FOR REGISTRATION: - Form 'B' for agent registration - Fees: Rs. 10,000 for 5 years - Professional qualification required - Pass qualifying exam RULE 12 - GRANT OF REGISTRATION: - Unique registration number - Valid for 5 years - Renewable RULE 13 - OBLIGATIONS OF AGENT: - Deal with registered projects only - Disclose all material facts - Maintain register of transactions - Submit annual returns RULE 14 - SUSPENSION/REVOCATION: - For violation of code of conduct - Complaints by buyers - Show cause notice procedure PART IV - COMPLAINT PROCEEDINGS (Rules 15-18) RULE 15 - MANNER OF COMPLAINT: - Form 'CRA' for complaint - Online submission - Fees: 1% of claim amount (max Rs. 5 lakhs) RULE 16 - PROCEDURE FOR HEARING: - Notice to respondent (30 days to reply) - Evidence by affidavit - Cross-examination allowed - Final hearing RULE 17 - TIME LIMIT FOR ORDERS: - 60 days from receipt of complaint - Extendable with reasons - Order in Form 'CRA-O' RULE 18 - APPEAL: - To Appellate Tribunal within 60 days - Deposit

as may be directed - Form 'APL' PART V - ADJUDICATION (Rules 19-21) RULE 19 - APPOINTMENT OF ADJUDICATING OFFICER: - By Authority - Powers to adjudicate compensation - Limit: Rs. 1 crore per complaint RULE 20 - PROCEDURE: - Natural justice principles - Evidence, cross-examination - Written orders with reasons RULE 21 - EXECUTION: - As decree of civil court - Through District Collector KEY FORMS: FORM A - Project Registration Application FORM B - Agent Registration Application FORM C - Quarterly Progress Report FORM CRA - Complaint Form FORM CRA-O - Order on Complaint FORM APL - Appeal Form MAHARASHTRA-SPECIFIC PROVISIONS: 1. INTEREST RATE (Rule 15): "Interest at the rate of State Bank of India highest marginal cost of lending rate plus 2% per annum" Currently: SBI MCLR (8.85%) + 2% = 10.85% per annum 2. BANK ACCOUNT (70% Rule): - Separate account for each project - 70% of collections deposited - Withdrawals proportionate to completion - Quarterly certificate by CA 3. CARPET AREA DEFINITION: Maharashtra follows central definition: - Net usable floor area - Excluding walls, ducts, balconies - Must be minimum 70% of saleable area 4. COMPLETION CERTIFICATE: - Occupancy Certificate by local authority - Completion Certificate by competent authority - Both required PENALTIES UNDER MAHARASHTRA RERA: Offense | Penalty --------|-------- Project non-registration | 10% of project cost Non-compliance with order | 5% of project cost + daily penalty Late quarterly report | Rs. 50,000 + Rs. 5,000 per day False information | Rs. 25 lakh Agent violation | Rs. 10,000 per day (max Rs. 5 lakh) No project website | Rs. 50,000 MAHARERA INNOVATIONS: ✓ Fully online system (paperless) ✓ Real-time project status updates ✓ SMS/email alerts to stakeholders ✓ Mobile app for complaints ✓ Fast-track disposal (average 6 months) ✓ Video conferencing hearings ✓ Published orders (transparency) MAHAR ERA STATISTICS (as of 2024): - Registered Projects: 50,000+ - Registered Agents: 25,000+ - Complaints Disposed: 20,000+ - Avg Disposal Time: 180 days - Success Rate (Buyers): 70% NOTABLE MAHARERA ORDERS: 1. Interest from booking date (not agreement date) 2. Refund includes stamp duty and registration 3. Builders can't cite COVID for entire delay 4. Grace period once only (not cumulative) 5. Delay in one tower affects all allottees' rights APPEALS TO HIGH COURT: From MahaRERA → Appellate Tribunal → Bombay High Court Bombay HC guidelines: - Limited interference - Only on law questions - Deposit required - Stay rare BEST PRACTICES: FOR BUYERS: ✓ Check project registration before booking ✓ Verify carpet area calculations ✓ Keep all payment records ✓ File quarterly status queries ✓ Complain immediately upon default FOR PROMOTERS: ✓ Complete registration before advertising ✓ Maintain 70% account strictly ✓ Submit quarterly reports on time ✓ Update website regularly ✓ Respond to complaints promptly CONTACT: Maharashtra RERA: - Address: 6th Floor, CIDCO Bhavan, CBD Belapur, Navi Mumbai - Phone: 022-27740200 - Email: complaints.rera@maharashtra.gov.in - Website: https://maharera.mahaonline.gov.in - Helpline: 1800-120-6666 (toll-free) Source: Maharashtra RERA Rules, 2017 Government Notification: Finance Department

RERA RULES - COMMON PROVISIONS ACROSS ALL STATES SOURCE: Comparative analysis of State RERA Rules (29 States + 7 UTs) BASED ON: RERA Act, 2016 (Central Legislation) UNIFORM PROVISIONS (All States): 1. REGISTRATION FEE STRUCTURE: Common Formula: 0.5% to 1% of estimated project cost Minimum: Rs. 50,000 to Rs. 1 lakh Maximum: Rs. 5 lakhs to Rs. 10 lakhs State-wise variations minimal. 2. AGENT REGISTRATION: Fee: Rs. 5,000 to Rs. 10,000 for 5 years Renewal: Same fee Exam: Mandatory in most states 3. INTEREST RATE (Section 18 & 19): UNIFORM FORMULA: State Bank of India MCLR + X% State | Rate ------|------ Maharashtra | MCLR + 2% Karnataka | MCLR + 2% Uttar Pradesh | MCLR + 1% Haryana | MCLR + 2% Rajasthan | MCLR + 2% Gujarat | MCLR + 2% Tamil Nadu | MCLR + 2% Delhi | MCLR + 2% Telangana | MCLR + 2% Madhya Pradesh | MCLR + 2% Current MCLR ~8.85%, so typical rate: 10.85% per annum 4. 70% BANK ACCOUNT RULE: All states implement Section 4(2)(l)(D): - 70% of collections in separate account - Project-wise accounts - Withdrawals certified by CA/Engineer - Proportionate to completion 5. CARPET AREA DEFINITION: Central Definition (Uniform): "Net usable floor area of an apartment, excluding area covered by external walls, areas under services shafts, exclusive balcony or verandah area and exclusive open terrace area, but includes areas covered by internal partition walls" Key: Balcony NOT included in carpet area. 6. QUARTERLY PROGRESS REPORT: All states mandate: - Physical progress percentage - Financial progress percentage - Architect/Engineer certification - Online submission - Non-compliance penalty 7. COMPLAINT FILING FEE: Typical: 1% of claim amount Minimum: Rs. 1,000 Maximum: Rs. 2 lakhs to Rs. 5 lakhs 8. TIME LIMIT FOR ORDERS: Target: 60 days (most states) Extendable: With recorded reasons Average actual disposal: 120-180 days 9. APPEAL PROVISIONS: Appeal to Appellate Tribunal: 60 days Appeal to High Court: 60 days (only on law) Deposit: 10-50% of awarded amount 10. ADJUDICATING OFFICER LIMIT: Uniform: Rs. 1 crore per complaint Beyond Rs. 1 crore: Civil court jurisdiction STATE-SPECIFIC VARIATIONS: FEATURE | VARIATIONS --------|------------ Online Portal | Maharashtra (best), Karnataka, UP (good), others (improving) Hearing Mode | Virtual hearings (post-COVID) - all states adopted Language | English + regional language forms Penalties | Minor variations in amounts Grace Period | Construction industry norm: 6-12 months (not in Act, but recognized) Force Majeure | COVID period exclusion (most states: Feb-June 2020) IMPLEMENTATION STATUS (State-wise): CATEGORY A - EXCELLENT IMPLEMENTATION: ✓ Maharashtra (MahaRERA) ✓ Karnataka (K-RERA) ✓ Uttar Pradesh (UP-RERA) ✓ Haryana (HRERA) ✓ Delhi (D-RERA) Features: Full online portal, fast disposal, published orders, mobile app CATEGORY B - GOOD IMPLEMENTATION: ✓ Gujarat, Tamil Nadu, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Telangana Features: Online portal, reasonable disposal time CATEGORY C - IMPROVING: West Bengal, Punjab, Kerala, Odisha, Bihar Features: Portal under development, manual processes coexist REGISTRATION REQUIREMENTS (Common): 1. LAND DOCUMENTS: - Title deed/agreement - Conveyance deed (if applicable) - Encumbrance certificate (30 years) - Land ownership proof

2. APPROVALS: - Building plan sanction - Commencement certificate - Environmental clearance (if required) - NOC from fire, aviation (if required) 3. FINANCIAL: - Project cost estimate (CA certified) - Proforma of agreement for sale - Specimen of allotment letter - Details of bank account 4. LEGAL: - Memorandum & Articles (if company) - Partnership deed (if partnership) - Board resolution authorizing registration - List of ongoing litigation - Affidavit on encumbrances EXEMPTIONS (Varies slightly by state): Generally NOT required to register: ✓ Renovation/repair without re-allotment ✓ Area < 500 sq.m. AND < 8 apartments ✓ Completion certificate received ✓ Projects completed before Act Some states exempt: - Government projects (some states) - Slum rehabilitation (Maharashtra) - Industrial/warehouse (some states) PENALTIES - RANGE ACROSS STATES: Violation | Minimum | Maximum ----------|---------|-------- Non-registration | Project cost 5% | Project cost 10% Order non-compliance | Rs. 10,000/day | Rs. 1 lakh/day Late progress report | Rs. 5,000/day | Rs. 50,000 flat False information | Rs. 1 lakh | 5% project cost Agent violation | Rs. 5,000/day | Rs. 10,000/day ADJUDICATION PROCEDURE (Common): 1. Complaint Filed → Registration → Notice to Respondent (15-30 days) 2. Reply Filed → Documents Exchanged → Evidence by Affidavit 3. Cross-Examination → Arguments → Final Hearing 4. Order Passed (with reasons) → Execution/Appeal EXECUTION MECHANISM: All states provide: - Recovery as public dues - Through District Collector - Attachment of properties - Prosecution for non-compliance TIME-BARRED COMPLAINTS: General position: - No specific limitation in Act - Typically 3 years from cause of action - Some states accept claims beyond 3 years - Authority discretion to condone delay MODEL AGREEMENT CLAUSES (Mandated): All states require promoter's agreement to include: 1. Clear possession date 2. Carpet area (not super built-up) 3. Specification of fittings 4. Common area percentage 5. Delay compensation clause 6. Payment plan clarity 7. Cancellation policy 8. Dispute resolution clause 9. RERA registration number DISCLOSURE REQUIREMENTS: Promoters must disclose (all states): ✓ RERA registration number on all docs ✓ Carpet area basis pricing ✓ Completion timeline ✓ Approval status ✓ Any litigation pending ✓ Any encumbrance on land ✓ Previous projects (completion status) BUYER RIGHTS (Uniform): ✓ Withdraw and get refund with interest ✓ OR stay and get interest till possession ✓ Compensation for delays ✓ Not to pay more than registered plans ✓ Changes only with 2/3rd allottees consent ✓ Rectification of defects (5 years) ✓ Fast-track dispute resolution RECENT DEVELOPMENTS (2023-2024): ✓ Online hearings normalized (post-COVID) ✓ SMS/Email updates to parties ✓ E-filing mandatory (most states) ✓ Mobile apps launched ✓ RERA integration with other govt portals ✓ Simplified forms ✓ Video-based inspections ✓ AI-assisted case management (pilots) CHALLENGES (Common across states): ✗ Pending case backlog (except Maharashtra) ✗ Limited authority resources ✗ Builders avoiding registration ✗ Inter-state project jurisdiction issues ✗ Enforcement of orders in other states ✗ Valuation disputes (fees calculation) BEST PRACTICES FROM LEADING STATES: FROM MAHARASHTRA: ✓ Complete online portal ✓ Public database of orders ✓ Fast disposal ✓ Proactive suo

moto actions FROM KARNATAKA: ✓ Detailed project progress tracking ✓ Quarterly compliance checks ✓ Builder rating system FROM UP: ✓ Simplified forms ✓ Vernacular language support ✓ Helpline integration USEFUL LINKS: Central RERA: https://rera.gov.in/ MahaRERA: https://maharera.mahaonline.gov.in/ K-RERA: https://rera.karnataka.gov.in/ UP-RERA: https://www.up-rera.in/ HRERA: https://haryanarera.gov.in/ D-RERA: https://rera.delhi.gov.in/ Source: Comparative Analysis of State RERA Rules (2017-2024)

CASE TITLE: Chand Rani and Ors vs Tata AIG General Insurance Co. Ltd and Anr COURT: District Judge (Comm.)-03 Shahdara, KKD, Delhi CASE NO: CS (Comm.) No. 221/22 JUDGE: Sh. Surinder S. Rathi DATE: 10 January 2024 DECISION: Dismissed ================================================================================ PARTIES ================================================================================ Plaintiffs: 1. Chand Rani (W/o Sh. Avinash Karir) 2. Suhani Karir (W/o Sh. Lucky Karir) 3. Sunny Kumar @ Sunny Defendants: 1. Tata AIG General Insurance Co. 2. Tata Capitals Financial Services Ltd. ================================================================================ SUBJECT MATTER ================================================================================ Suit for recovery of Rs. 16,72,600/- with interest @ 16% per annum and mandatory injunction. ================================================================================ FACTS ================================================================================ 1. Plaintiffs claimed deceased Lucky Karir purchased property (Flat No. G-167 C/F1, Dilshad Garden Extension-1, Delhi) with plaintiff No. 1 on 10.02.2004. 2. Lucky Karir applied for loan against property with defendant No. 2 on 24.07.2019, sanctioned on 04.09.2019 for Rs. 20.10 lacs, repayable in 180 EMIs of Rs. 23,081/-. 3. Lucky Karir required to pay Rs. 60,000/- to defendant No. 1 for Group Credit Secure Plus Policy (Rs. 16,600/- for five years: 13.09.2019 to 12.09.2024). 4. Lucky Karir died on 20.10.2019. 5. Insurance claim rejected on 15.11.2019. 6. Defendant No. 2 issued loan recall notice on 12.02.2020 and Section 13(2) SARFAESI Act notice on 18.02.2022. ================================================================================ DEFENDANTS' CASE ================================================================================ Defendant No. 1 (Insurance Company): - Issued policy for Rs. 16,72,600/- effective 13.09.2019 to 12.09.2024 - Learned on 08.11.2019 that Lucky Karir diagnosed with Cancer on 10.10.2019 and died on 20.10.2019 - As per Clause 1(b) of policy, death from Cancer within 90 days of policy issuance NOT COVERED - Claim rejected on 15.11.2019 Defendant No. 2 (Finance Company): - Entered appearance on 06.08.2022 - Filed application under Order 7 Rule 11 CPC but did not file written statement within prescribed period ================================================================================ ISSUES FRAMED ================================================================================ PRELIMINARY ISSUE: Whether suit deserves dismissal for concealment of material facts and pleading false facts? OTHER ISSUES: 1. Whether defendant No. 1 justified in rejecting insurance claim? 2. Whether suit hit by Section 34 of SARFAESI Act? 3. Whether plaintiffs entitled to decree of Rs. 16,72,600/- with interest? 4. Whether plaintiffs entitled to injunction against dispossession? ================================================================================ EVIDENCE ================================================================================ Plaintiff's Evidence: PW-1 Chand Rani deposed via affidavit, exhibiting loan agreement, insurance certificate, sanction letter, death certificate and other documents. Cross-examination revealed deceased had widow and two minor children. Defendant's Evidence: DW-1 Nidhi Kalra (Chief Manager, Tata AIG) confirmed policy details, premium payment of Rs. 60,000/-, and that no medical examination conducted before policy issuance. Admitted policy issued within two days of premium receipt. ================================================================================ LEGAL ANALYSIS ================================================================================ PRELIMINARY ISSUE - CONCEALMENT OF FACTS: Court found MATERIAL CONCEALMENT. Plaint stated only Lucky Karir applied for and availed loan, but loan agreement (Ex. PW1/2) showed FOUR CO-APPLICANTS: Lucky Karir, Chand Rani, Suhani Karir, and Sunny Karir. All three plaintiffs filed FALSE AFFIDAVITS under Order 6 Rule 15A(5) CPC stating: "there is no false statement or concealment of any material fact". Court relied on multiple Supreme Court precedents: S.P. CHENGALVARAYA NAIDU (1984): "One who comes to the court, must come

with clean hands...a person whose case is based on falsehood has no right to approach the court." MORGAN STANLEY MUTUAL FUND (1994): Courts must "discourage speculative and vexatious litigation and judicial adventurism." KISHORE SAMRITE (2013): Courts should burden litigants abusing process with "exemplary and deterrent cost." DALIP SINGH (2021): "litigant, who attempts to pollute the stream of justice...is not entitled to any relief, interim or final." CONCLUSION: Concealment was not poor drafting but "clever drafting so as to evade payment of defaulted loan amount...under the garb of death of one of the four co-borrowers." ISSUE 1 - INSURANCE CLAIM REJECTION: UNDISPUTED FACTS: Policy issued 13.09.2019, Lucky Karir died 20.10.2019 (37 days later) from Cancer, claim rejected 15.11.2019 citing Clause 1(b). PLAINTIFFS ARGUED: (1) Policy terms never supplied (2) Deceased did not die of Cancer COURT REJECTED BOTH: 1. Insurance Certificate (Page 51, Ex. PW1/3) stated: "this is only a summary...actual benefits...in the enclosed policy wordings...subject to policy terms, conditions and exclusion." 2. Plaint mentioned death "due to illness" without using "Cancer". WS categorically stated plaintiffs informed insurer of Cancer death. No replication filed rebutting this. No medical documents produced. No suggestion to DW-1 that death wasn't from Cancer. Court drew ADVERSE INFERENCE under Section 114(g) Evidence Act. Court cited SHREE AMBICA MEDICAL STORES (2020): "Court has to simply apply the terms and conditions of the agreement as agreed between the parties" and cannot "rewrite or create a new contract." FINDING: Defendant No. 1 "well within its right to decline the claim." ISSUES 2 & 4 - SARFAESI BAR AND INJUNCTION: Prayer 2 sought injunction restraining defendant No. 2 from taking possession of mortgaged property. Court noted Section 34 SARFAESI Act bars civil court jurisdiction for disputes over Rs. 20 lacs, which fall under DRT jurisdiction. Loan was Rs. 20.10 lacs. Plaintiff's counsel conceded legal position and admitted DRT proceedings already initiated. FINDING: Prayer No. 2 BARRED before Civil/Commercial Court. ISSUE 3 - DECREE FOR RS. 16,72,600/-: Court held: 1. Insurance claim properly rejected per policy terms 2. Plaintiffs failed to discharge onus of proof 3. Preliminary issue decided against plaintiffs (concealment) 4. Plaintiffs not entitled to any relief ================================================================================ FINAL ORDER ================================================================================ SUIT DISMISSED. All issues decided against plaintiffs. COSTS: Parties to bear their own costs. PERJURY: Despite false affidavits warranting perjury proceedings, Court took lenient view considering plaintiff No. 1 is 66-year-old widow and plaintiff No. 2 is widow with two minor children. NO PERJURY PROCEEDINGS INITIATED. REASONING: "while it is correct that complete true facts were not pleaded but the loan documents were filed, according to which, it is evident that the loan was availed by four co-borrowers." ================================================================================ KEY LEGAL PRINCIPLES ================================================================================ 1. CLEAN HANDS DOCTRINE: Litigants must approach courts with clean hands; material concealment justifies summary dismissal. 2. INSURANCE CONTRACTS: Interpreted strictly per terms agreed; courts cannot rewrite insurance contracts. 3. ADVERSE INFERENCE: Section 114(g) Evidence Act - Adverse inference drawn from non-production of documents. 4. SARFAESI JURISDICTION: Civil courts lack jurisdiction over SARFAESI matters exceeding

Rs. 20 lacs. 5. POLICY EXCLUSIONS: Death from pre-existing conditions within exclusion period validly grounds for claim rejection. 6. BURDEN OF PROOF: Claimant must prove all elements of claim including cause of death falls within policy coverage. 7. FALSE AFFIDAVITS: Filing false verification affidavits constitutes serious misconduct warranting dismissal and potential perjury proceedings. ================================================================================ Source: Indian Kanoon (indiankanoon.org/doc/45845725/) Downloaded: October 2026

CASE: Sunil Kumar Sengar & Anr. vs M/S. Unitech Ltd. COURT: National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission YEAR: 2015 CITATION: indiankanoon.org/doc/2398732/ KEY ISSUE: Delayed possession and compensation in real estate project FACTS: - Complainants booked residential units with Unitech Ltd. - Agreement executed with specified possession date - Builder failed to deliver possession within agreed timeline - Sought refund and compensation for delay and harassment CONSUMER PROTECTION ACT PROVISIONS: - Section 2(1)(d) - Definition of consumer - Section 2(1)(g) - Deficiency in service - Unfair trade practice by developer RELIEF SOUGHT: 1. Refund of entire amount paid with interest 2. Compensation for mental agony and harassment 3. Litigation costs DEFICIENCY IN SERVICE: - Non-delivery of possession as per agreement - Inordinate delay without valid reason - Mental harassment caused to consumers - Violation of consumer rights PRINCIPLES: - Builders must honor possession timelines - Delay constitutes deficiency in service - Consumers entitled to compensation - Interest payable from date of booking till refund TYPICAL AWARDS: - Refund of principal amount - Interest @ 9-12% per annum - Compensation Rs. 50,000 - Rs. 2,00,000 for mental agony - Litigation costs SIGNIFICANCE: National Consumer Forum consistently holds developers accountable for delayed possession. Establishes consumer rights in real estate sector before RERA Act came into force. Source: Indian Kanoon Category: Consumer Protection - Real Estate Disputes

CASE: Union Of India, General Manager vs S.C. Mariappan COURT: State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission YEAR: 2022 CITATION: indiankanoon.org/doc/199928702/ KEY ISSUE: Deficiency in government service delivery FACTS: - Complainant availed government service - Deficiency in service delivery by Union of India/Government entity - Consumer forum found service provider liable - Government entity challenged the order LEGAL POSITION: - Government entities providing services are subject to Consumer Protection Act - No immunity for government departments from consumer complaints - Service deficiency principles apply equally to public and private entities CONSUMER PROTECTION ACT 2019: - Section 2(42) - "Service" includes services provided by government - Section 2(7) - Definition of "consumer" - Government not exempted from consumer protection obligations DEFICIENCY GROUNDS: - Unreasonable delay in service delivery - Negligence in performing duties - Inadequate response to complaints - Mental harassment to consumer COMPENSATION PRINCIPLES: - Actual loss suffered - Mental agony (typically Rs. 10,000 - Rs. 50,000) - Litigation costs - Interest on delayed payments KEY LEGAL PRINCIPLES: 1. Government departments providing services are "service providers" 2. Delay beyond reasonable time constitutes deficiency 3. Consumer forums have jurisdiction over government entities 4. Compensation includes actual loss + mental agony PRECEDENTS RELIED: - Secretary, PWD vs P. Ravindran (1997) - Government bodies not exempt - Indian Medical Association vs VP Shantha (1995) - Service definition - Lucknow Development Authority cases - Government amenability SIGNIFICANCE: Reaffirms that government entities must comply with consumer protection standards. Citizens can seek redressal for government service deficiency through consumer forums. Source: Indian Kanoon Category: Consumer Protection - Government Services

CASE TITLE: CCI Projects Private Limited Mumbai vs Rajesh Kumar Chaudhary And Anr COURT: Bombay High Court - Civil Appellate Jurisdiction CASE NO: Second Appeal No. 479 of 2021 CITATION: 2026:BHC-AS:9416 DATE OF JUDGMENT: 18 June, 2026 BENCH: Justice Sharmila U. Deshmukh ================================================================================ PARTIES ================================================================================ Appellant/Promoter: CCI Projects Private Limited, Office at Rivali Park, CCI Compound, Western Express Highway, Borivali East, Mumbai 400 066 Respondents/Allottees: 1. Mr. Rajesh Kumar Chaudhary 2. Mrs. Sapna Chaudhary (Plus 5 other respondents) ================================================================================ FACTS ================================================================================ 1. Allottees booked apartment in "Wintergreen" building, project "Ekta Meadows" developed by Promoters 2. Allotment letter dated 1st October, 2011 mentioned possession date as 30th June, 2015 with six months grace period 3. Agreement dated 26th March, 2013 stipulated possession by February 2016 (Clause 17) 4. Total consideration: Rs. 1,82,18,640/-; Amount paid: Rs. 1,91,59,215/- (including taxes) 5. Possession not handed over by agreed date 6. RERA registration showed proposed completion: 31st December, 2018; revised to 31st December, 2019 7. Complaint filed on 23rd May, 2018 under Section 31 of RERA Act ================================================================================ PROCEEDINGS BELOW ================================================================================ MahaRERA Order (17th September, 2018): Directed promoter to handover apartments with occupancy certificate before 31st December, 2019. Allowed allottees liberty to demand interest at appropriate stage under Section 18 of RERA Act. Appellate Tribunal Order (10th March, 2021): - Quashed MahaRERA order - Directed promoter to pay interest @ SBI MCLR plus 2% from 1st March, 2016 till possession - Awarded costs of Rs. 25,000/- - Found no evidence of allottees accepting revised possession date - Held unilateral extension by promoter not binding on allottees Actual Possession: - Occupation certificate obtained: 7th April, 2021 - Possession offered: 13th April, 2021 - Possession taken: 18th June, 2021 ================================================================================ SUBSTANTIAL QUESTIONS OF LAW ================================================================================ 1. Whether acceptance of delayed performance under Section 55 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 disentitles the promisee from compensation for non-performance at agreed time? 2. Whether Section 18 of the Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016 overrides Section 55 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872? 3. Whether force majeure events in the contract could be ignored under Section 32 of Indian Contract Act, 1872? ================================================================================ KEY ARGUMENTS ================================================================================ Appellant's Submissions: 1. ACCEPTANCE OF DELAYED PERFORMANCE: "allottees by their conduct had accepted the substituted performance" through: - Letter dated 15th April, 2015 informing delay till March 2018 - Letter dated 14th March, 2017 revising possession to December 2018 - Letter dated 9th June, 2017 revising payment schedule - Payment of 5% installment on 30th March, 2018 per revised schedule - Letter dated 19th August, 2017 stating final delivery December 2019 2. SECTION 55 CONTRACT ACT APPLICATION: "if the party chooses to remain silent, he forfeits his right to contend that he did not agree to the revised date." Notice of intention to claim compensation required at time of accepting delayed performance. 3. FORCE MAJEURE: COVID-19 circular dated 18th May, 2020 provided six-month moratorium (1st February to 30th June, 2020) to be excluded from interest calculation. Respondents' Submissions: 1. UNILATERAL EXTENSION INVALID:

"unilateral extension of revised date of possession by the promoter is not binding upon the allottees" - no evidence of acceptance. 2. RERA OVERRIDES CONTRACT ACT: Section 18 RERA is "express provision" conferring statutory right to interest; RERA is special Act overriding general Contract Act. 3. CONSTRUCTION-LINKED PAYMENTS: Payments were milestone-based, not date-specific, so "delay of construction meant delayed payments" - no acceptance of revised dates. 4. ABSOLUTE RIGHT: Citing Newtech Promoters: "The unqualified right of the allottee to seek refund...is not dependent on any contingencies or stipulations thereof." 5. COVID CIRCULAR INAPPLICABLE: Possession due pre-COVID, so moratorium doesn't apply. ================================================================================ LEGAL PROVISIONS CITED ================================================================================ RERA Act, 2016: - Section 3 (Registration of projects) - Section 18 (Return of amount and compensation) - Section 31 (Complaint to Authority) - Section 88 (Application of other laws) - Section 89 (Overriding effect) Indian Contract Act, 1872: - Section 32 (Force majeure) - Section 55 (Effect of failure to perform at fixed time) - Section 62 (Novation) ================================================================================ COURT'S FINDINGS AND REASONING ================================================================================ 1. ON SECTION 18 RERA - NATURE OF RIGHT: "Plain reading of Section 18 does not indicate that the rights conferred on the allottee upon failure of the promoter...is qualified by any contingency." Citing Newtech Promoters: "The unqualified right of the allottee...is not dependent on any contingencies or stipulations thereof...regardless of unforeseen events or stay orders." HELD: "the right of allottee under Section 18(1)(a)...is unqualified right not affected by any contingencies." 2. ON ACCEPTANCE OF DELAYED PERFORMANCE: "The revised timelines were unilateral and the contention...of acceptance of delayed performance is premised on the basis that by accepting the revised dates of payment...the allottees have accepted the delayed performance by their conduct." However: "The payment schedule agreed between the parties was construction linked payments and not linked to specific dates. Unless and until, the specified construction was carried out, no right accrued to the promoter to claim any money." CONCLUSION: "Even accepting that there was acceptance of revised date of possession, considering Section 18 of RERA Act, the allottees were well within their rights to accept the delayed performance without foregoing their right to interest." 3. ON SECTION 55 CONTRACT ACT vs SECTION 18 RERA: "Section 55 of Contract Act permits the same option to the promisee...but qualifies the right to claim compensation only upon giving notice while accepting delayed performance." CRITICAL DISTINCTION: "If the right under Section 18 of RERA Act is an unqualified absolute right, the acceptance of revised timelines and delayed performance cannot lay fetters on the right to claim interest." ON CONFLICT: "Whereas Section 18 of RERA Act gives an unqualified absolute statutory right...Section 55 of Contract Act lays fetters on that right making it subject to giving notice." 4. ON OVERRIDING EFFECT: "RERA Act being a special enactment will prevail over Contract Act, a general law. Section 89 of RERA Act gives it an overriding effect over anything inconsistent with the other laws." Citing Newtech Promoters: "the legislature consciously enacted a retroactive statute" and "negated the

contention of the contractual terms having an overriding effect over the retrospective applicability of the Act." 5. ON FORCE MAJEURE/COVID-19: "Covid 19 pandemic falls within the ambit of force majeure clause. The date of handing over possession...was February, 2016...The force majeure event of Covid-19 was subsequent to the due date of performance." Following Pragatej Builders: "where the possession was to be handed over before the Covid-19 pandemic...the subsequent Covid-19 pandemic, lockdown cannot come to the aid of the promoter." 6. ON SUMMARY JURISDICTION: "The decision makes it clear that the legislative intent was to invest the Regulatory Authority with the jurisdiction to decide the complaints under Section 18...by conducting summary nature of scrutiny of undisputed facts." ================================================================================ JUDGMENT AND ORDER ================================================================================ ANSWERS TO SUBSTANTIAL QUESTIONS: (a) Question 1: "Under the provisions of Section 18 of RERA Act, the handing over possession as per terms of agreement...is sacrosanct remaining unqualified by any contingencies...and is not affected by the acceptance of delayed performance." (b) Question 2: "Section 89 of RERA Act gives it an overriding effect over anything inconsistent with the other laws and the retroactive application of RERA Act would impose an obligation on the promoter to pay interest...even in the absence of any notice to the promoter." (c) Question 3: "The aspect of seeking benefit of moratorium is covered by decision of this Court...and being settled does not give rise to substantial question of law." FINAL ORDER: 1. Second Appeal DISMISSED 2. Appellate Tribunal's order dated 10th March, 2021 UPHELD: - Promoter to pay interest @ SBI MCLR + 2% from 1st March, 2016 till possession date (18th June, 2021) - Promoter to pay Rs. 25,000/- as costs 3. Execution proceedings stayed for 4 weeks from 24th June, 2026 4. All pending applications disposed of ================================================================================ KEY LEGAL PRINCIPLES ESTABLISHED ================================================================================ 1. UNQUALIFIED RIGHT UNDER RERA: Section 18 confers absolute, unconditional statutory right to interest unaffected by acceptance of delayed performance or lack of notice. 2. RERA OVERRIDES CONTRACT ACT: Where inconsistency exists between Section 18 RERA and Section 55 Contract Act on compensation rights, RERA prevails as special legislation with Section 89 overriding effect. 3. RETROACTIVE APPLICATION: RERA applies to pre-RERA agreements; statutory obligations imposed regardless of contractual terms or subsequent revisions. 4. AGREED DATE SACROSANCT: Date specified in agreement for possession remains binding; unilateral extensions by promoter not binding without formal amendment. 5. FORCE MAJEURE TIMING: Force majeure events occurring after due date of performance cannot benefit defaulting party; COVID-19 moratorium inapplicable where possession due pre-pandemic. 6. SUMMARY JURISDICTION: RERA Authority empowered to conduct summary inquiry on undisputed facts without elaborate adjudication process required for Contract Act claims. ================================================================================ Source: Indian Kanoon (indiankanoon.org/doc/76954287/) Downloaded: October 2026

CASE TITLE: CCI Projects Private Limited Mumbai vs Sriram Krishnan COURT: High Court of Judicature at Bombay CASE NO: Second Appeal No. 472 of 2021 BENCH: Hon'ble Justice Sharmila U. Deshmukh DATE: Pronounced on 18th June, 2026 ================================================================================ PARTIES ================================================================================ Appellant: CCI Projects Private Limited (Promoter) Office at Rivali Park, CCI Compound, Western Express Highway, Borivali East, Mumbai 400 066 Respondents: 1. Mr. Sriram Krishnan (Allottee) 2. Mrs. Vidya Sriram (Allottee) 3-7. Other Directors/Officers of CCI Projects ================================================================================ FACTS ================================================================================ 1. Allottees booked apartment in "Wintergreen" building developed by Promoters 2. Agreement executed on 18th November, 2014 3. Clause 17: Possession to be given on or before 30th June, 2017 4. Total consideration: Rs. 1,95,06,060/- 5. Amount paid by allottees: Rs. 2,05,89,715/- (including taxes) 6. RERA registration proposed completion: 31st December, 2018 (revised to 31st December, 2019) 7. Possession not delivered by due date ================================================================================ PROCEEDINGS BEFORE LOWER AUTHORITIES ================================================================================ MahaRERA Order (31st January, 2019): - Directed possession by 31st December, 2019 - Liberty to allottees to demand interest at appropriate stage under Section 18 RERA Appellate Tribunal Order (10th March, 2021): - Quashed MahaRERA order - Directed payment of interest @ SBI MCLR + 2% from 1st July, 2017 till possession - Cost of Rs. 25,000/- to allottees ================================================================================ SUBSTANTIAL QUESTIONS OF LAW ================================================================================ (i) Whether acceptance of delayed performance under Section 55 of Indian Contract Act, 1872 disentitles promisee from compensation for non-performance at agreed time? (ii) Whether Section 18 of RERA Act, 2016 overrides Section 55 of Contract Act? (iii) Whether force majeure events in contract could be ignored under Section 32 of Contract Act? (iv) Whether appeals maintainable given allottees' concession that interest would be considered after project completion? ================================================================================ KEY LEGAL PROVISIONS ================================================================================ Section 18 RERA (Return of amount and compensation): "(1) If the promoter fails to complete or is unable to give possession of an apartment... (a) in accordance with the terms of the agreement for sale or...by the date specified therein... Provided that where an allottee does not intend to withdraw from the project, he shall be paid, by the promoter, interest for every month of delay, till the handing over of the possession, at such rate as may be prescribed." Section 55 Indian Contract Act: Effect of failure to perform at fixed time; acceptance of delayed performance Section 88 RERA: RERA provisions in addition to other enactments Section 89 RERA: Overriding effect over inconsistent laws ================================================================================ JUDICIAL ANALYSIS & FINDINGS ================================================================================ 1. SECTION 18 RERA - NATURE OF RIGHT: The Court held: "Section 18 gives unqualified, unconditional absolute right to allottees" Citing Newtech Promoters: "without prejudice to any other remedy available...if the allottee does not intend to withdraw...entitled to and must be paid interest" Key Points: - Right under Section 18 "not dependent on any contingencies or stipulations" - Allottees can accept delayed performance without foregoing interest rights - Notice not required under Section 18 unlike Section 55 - Agreement date for possession remains sacrosanct 2. RERA OVERRIDE OF CONTRACT ACT: Court

found: - Retroactive operation: RERA applies to ongoing projects registered under Section 3 - Inconsistency identified: Section 18 gives unqualified right; Section 55 conditions it on notice - Special law prevails: RERA as special enactment prevails over general Contract Act - Section 89 effect: RERA has "overriding effect over anything inconsistent with the other laws" - Contractual terms subordinate: Supreme Court in Newtech "negated the contention of the contractual terms having an overriding effect" 3. FORCE MAJEURE: - COVID-19 irrelevant: Pandemic occurred after June 2017 due date and December 2019 RERA date - Precedent binding: M/s Pragatej Builders decision holds possession due before COVID cannot claim relief for pandemic 4. MAINTAINABILITY OF APPEAL: - No express waiver of rights by allottees - Plea of parity is not concession waiving statutory rights - Statutory right to interest cannot be waived by advocate's concession on law ================================================================================ FINAL ORDER ================================================================================ The Court: 1. DISMISSED Second Appeal 2. ANSWERED SUBSTANTIAL QUESTIONS: (a) Acceptance of delayed performance does not disentitle allottees from interest under Section 18 (b) Section 18 RERA overrides Section 55 Contract Act on compensation claim (c) Force majeure not applicable; COVID occurred post-due date (d) Appeal maintainable; no concession waiving statutory rights 3. STAYED EXECUTION: 4 weeks from 24th June 2026 4. UPHELD Appellate Tribunal order: Interest @ SBI MCLR + 2% from 1st July 2017 till possession 5. COSTS: Rs. 25,000/- to allottees ================================================================================ KEY LEGAL PRINCIPLES ESTABLISHED ================================================================================ 1. RERA Section 18 creates unqualified absolute right to interest for delayed possession 2. Acceptance of revised payment schedules does not constitute acceptance of revised possession dates 3. Legislative intent in RERA is summary adjudication, not detailed inquiry into contractual modifications 4. Special statute (RERA) prevails over general law (Contract Act) where inconsistent 5. Retroactive RERA application imposes obligations regardless of pre-RERA agreements 6. Date in registered agreement remains sacrosanct reference for Section 18 calculation 7. No estoppel against statutory rights even if advocate makes concession on law point 8. Plea of parity is not concession waiving substantive rights ================================================================================ The judgment reinforces consumer protection under RERA and limits contractual arrangements that could dilute statutory protections for homebuyers.
