CASE TITLE: Macrotech Developers Ltd. vs Suryakant Yashwant Jadhav & Ors COURT: High Court of Judicature at Bombay - Civil Appellate Jurisdiction CASE NO: Second Appeal No. 297 of 2021 and Second Appeal No. 298 of 2021 BENCH: Hon'ble Justice Sharmila U. Deshmukh DATE: Reserved: April 9, 2026 | Pronounced: June 8, 2026 ================================================================================ PARTIES ================================================================================ Appellant/Applicant: Macrotech Developers Ltd. (earlier known as Bellissima Hi-Rise Builders Pvt. Ltd.) Registered Office: Lodha Excelus, N.M. Joshi Marg, Mahalakshmi, Mumbai - 400 011 Respondents: 1. Suryakant Yashwant Jadhav 2. Suryakant Jadhav HUF 3. Bankim Ashok Doshi 4. Sushant Keru Hirve 5. Palava Dwellers Pvt. Ltd. ================================================================================ FACTS ================================================================================ 1. Respondents booked two apartments (Flat Nos. 901-H and 902-H) in Appellant's project "Palava Lakeside A to H" situated at Palava, Kalyan. 2. Agreements for Sale duly executed and registered between parties in May 2014, prior to enactment of RERA. 3. Respondents paid approximately 95-96% of purchase consideration. 4. As per Annexure-2 of flat purchaser's agreement, date of offer of possession for fit-outs specified as February 28, 2017. 5. Claiming delay in possession, Respondents sent communications dated March 22, 2018 and May 14, 2018, ultimately withdrawing from project on May 14, 2018. 6. Appellant sent communication on June 21, 2018 offering possession of flats. 7. Respondents filed application under Section 18 of RERA before MahaRERA seeking refund with interest and compensation. 8. Adjudicating Authority-MahaRERA rejected application vide order dated March 6, 2019. 9. Maharashtra Real Estate Appellate Tribunal allowed appeal vide judgment dated January 12, 2021, directing refund with interest. ================================================================================ KEY CONTRACTUAL CLAUSES ================================================================================ Clause 1.13: Defined date of offer of possession for fit-outs as per Annexure-2 (February 28, 2017) Clause 1.14: Defined date of offer of possession as the date OC is issued Clause 11.1: "The Company shall endeavor to provide the Unit...for fit outs on or before the date as set out in Annexure '2'...within a period of 1 (One) year" Clause 11.2: "The Company shall...be entitled to a grace period of 1 (One) year beyond the aforesaid dates mentioned in Clause 11.1" Clause 11.3: Provided option to purchaser to terminate agreement within 90 days of expiry of grace period if possession for fit-outs delayed ================================================================================ ARGUMENTS ================================================================================ Appellant's Contentions: 1. Date of possession should be linked to date of issuance of Occupation Certificate (OC), which was received on May 10, 2018. 2. Agreement provided for grace period of one year beyond dates specified, making outer limit for possession February 28, 2019. 3. Possession was offered on June 21, 2018, within contractually agreed period including grace period. 4. Section 18 of RERA not applicable as there was no delay in handing over possession as per agreement terms. 5. Appellate Tribunal erred in disregarding grace period clause and holding it contrary to RERA. Respondents' Contentions: 1. Possession was to be handed over on February 28, 2017, and delay entitled them to withdraw from project. 2. Communication of June 21, 2018 made no mention of OC and architect's certificate of same date stated buildings

were under construction. 3. Grace period provision is unqualified under Section 18 of RERA. 4. Relying on Venkataraman Krishnamurthy & Anr. vs Lodha Crown Buildmart Pvt. Ltd., Respondents argued they were entitled to withdraw within grace period. 5. Architect's certificate confirmed only fit-out possession was initiated on June 21, 2018. ================================================================================ SUBSTANTIAL QUESTIONS OF LAW ================================================================================ 1. Whether complaint filed by Respondents before MahaRERA is maintainable under Section 18 of RERA Act? 2. Whether clause in flat purchaser's agreement providing for grace period is contrary to statutory provisions of RERA? 3. Whether flat purchaser is entitled to withdraw from project within grace period upon failure of developer to adhere to date of handing over possession? ================================================================================ LEGAL PROVISIONS CITED ================================================================================ Section 18(1) of RERA: "If the promoter fails to complete or is unable to give possession of an apartment...in accordance with the terms of the agreement for sale or...by the date specified therein...the allottee...may...withdraw from the project...to return the amount received...with interest...including compensation" ================================================================================ JUDGMENT AND REASONING ================================================================================ ON MAINTAINABILITY (Question 1): Court held that Section 18 gives primacy to agreement terms. Date of final possession must be determined as per Clause 11.1 read with Annexure-2. Court applied interpretation from Venkataraman Krishnamurthy & Anr. vs Lodha Crown Buildmart Pvt. Ltd., holding that: - Date of possession for fit-outs: February 28, 2017, extended to February 28, 2018 (with grace period) - Date of final possession: One year from fit-out possession date = February 28, 2018 (without additional grace period) Court ruled: "Where the Appellant failed to hand over possession for fit outs by 28th February, 2018, the Appellants cannot take disadvantage of their own failure" Since possession not handed over by February 28, 2018, application under Section 18 was maintainable. ON GRACE PERIOD VALIDITY (Question 2): Court noted agreements were executed in 2014, pre-RERA. There is no statutory embargo under MOFA preventing parties from deciding computation of final possession date. Court concluded: "The question as framed, in view of the factual scenario of the agreements being pre-RERA does not arise for consideration" ON RIGHT TO WITHDRAW (Question 3): Court held Respondents were entitled to withdraw under both Section 18 of RERA and Clause 11.3 of agreement. Withdrawal on May 14, 2018 was within 90 days of expiry of grace period for fit-out possession (February 28, 2018). Architect's certificate dated June 21, 2018 confirmed buildings were under construction, contradicting claims of timely completion. ================================================================================ FINAL ORDER ================================================================================ 1. Second Appeals DISMISSED. 2. Order of Maharashtra Real Estate Appellate Tribunal dated January 12, 2021 UPHELD. 3. Appellant directed to refund amounts received from Respondents along with interest. 4. Respondents have liberty to file petition for compensation before Adjudicating Officer under Sections 71 and 72 of RERA. 5. Interim Applications disposed of. ================================================================================ KEY LEGAL PRINCIPLES ================================================================================ 1. SECTION 18 RERA - AGREEMENT TERMS PRIMACY: Section 18 gives primacy to agreement terms in determining date of possession for purposes of determining delay. 2. GRACE PERIOD INTERPRETATION: Grace period for fit-out possession does not extend

to final possession timeline; developer cannot take advantage of own delay. 3. RIGHT TO WITHDRAW: Allottees entitled to withdraw within grace period when possession for fit-outs not provided by stipulated date. 4. PRE-RERA AGREEMENTS: Pre-RERA agreements subject to RERA provisions once Act comes into force for ongoing projects. 5. ARCHITECT'S CERTIFICATE: Certificate stating buildings under construction contradicts claim of timely possession offer. 6. COMPENSATION REMEDY: Allottees who withdraw retain right to seek compensation under Sections 71-72 RERA before Adjudicating Officer. ================================================================================ Justice Sharmila U. Deshmukh Bombay High Court June 8, 2026 Source: Indian Kanoon (indiankanoon.org/doc/82878576/) Downloaded: October 2026

CASE TITLE: Omaxe Ltd vs Mr. Joginder Singh Nijjar & Anr COURT: High Court of Delhi at New Delhi CASE NO: FAO(OS) (COMM) 236/2023 BENCH: Hon'ble Mr. Justice V. Kameswar Rao and Hon'ble Ms. Justice Manmeet Pritam Singh Arora DATE: Reserved: 22 July, 2026 | Pronounced: 14 August, 2026 ================================================================================ PARTIES ================================================================================ Appellant: Omaxe Ltd. Respondents: Mr. Joginder Singh Nijjar & Anr. Counsel for Appellant: Sh. Ramesh Singh, Senior Advocate with Mr. Mukti Bodh, Ms. Mala Diwadi, Ms. Nanya Hage, and Ms. Neha Chaturvedi Counsel for Respondents: Ms. Shobhana Takiar with Mr. Shivam Takiar, Mr. Prateek Dhir, and Mr. Kuljeet Singh ================================================================================ INTRODUCTION ================================================================================ This appeal challenges judgment dated 19.07.2023 dismissing Appellant's Section 34 petition against Arbitral Award dated 20.03.2020. The Award directed refund of Rs. 3,35,04,650/- (principal) plus Rs. 4,16,94,674/- (pendente lite interest), totaling Rs. 7,51,99,324/-, with future interest at 12% and costs of Rs. 25 lakhs. Dispute arose from Allotment Agreement dated 02.05.2008 for Commercial Unit No. 26 in 'Omaxe Novelty Mall', Amritsar. Sole Arbitrator was Justice B.S. Chauhan (Retd.), appointed by Supreme Court. ================================================================================ FACTUAL BACKGROUND ================================================================================ 1. Appellant developed commercial project pursuant to Collaboration Agreement dated 23.05.2005. Municipal Corporation sanctioned construction up to 30 meters height on 25.05.2006. 2. Respondents applied for allotment on 10.02.2007 and paid Rs. 10,05,13,952/- (95% of basic sale price) by 26.11.2007. Allotment Agreement executed on 02.05.2008 for five co-allottees, with Respondents holding 33.33% jointly. 3. Addendum dated 02.05.2008 provided for monthly assured returns of Rs. 9,84,199/- (9% return) until possession. Payments made from 29.11.2007 to 30.04.2010, then discontinued. 4. Agreement stipulated 36 months construction period from 02.05.2008, expiring 01.05.2011. Appellant failed to complete by this date. Respondents issued termination notice on 18.04.2013 seeking refund and arbitration. 5. Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) objected that project fell within regulated area of Maharaja Ranjit Singh Summer Palace. Construction beyond 15 meters stopped. ASI later permitted construction up to 24 meters on 22.02.2012. Construction remained stalled from April 2007 to February 2012. 6. Completion Certificate issued on 08.07.2015 but cancelled on 29.01.2016. High Court of Punjab and Haryana stayed cancellation on 17.02.2016, and Certificate restored on 31.07.2019. Appellant offered possession on 16.07.2015, 21.11.2015, and 18.02.2017. 7. Respondents rejected possession offers and sought arbitration. Supreme Court appointed Justice B.S. Chauhan (Retd.) as Sole Arbitrator on 17.09.2018. Arbitral Award dated 20.03.2020 awarded refund with interest. ================================================================================ APPELLANT'S SUBMISSIONS ================================================================================ 1. Arbitral Tribunal erred in upholding termination despite project completion and possession offers. Time was never essence of contract; no notice making time essential issued. 2. Addendum provided for assured returns contemplating delay. Clause 26(e) stipulated compensation of Rs. 10 per sq. ft. per month for delay, excluding termination rights. Reliance on Section 55, Indian Contract Act, 1872. 3. Delay period during ASI restrictions (2008-2012) constituted force majeure under Clause 26(b), being beyond Appellant's control. 4. Termination notice dated 18.04.2013 issued by only two of five co-allottees despite joint and indivisible allotment. Non-joinder fatal. 5. Interest at 14% contradicts contractual stipulation of 6%. Force majeure period and

post-offer period should be excluded. Rs. 2,85,71,431/- paid as assured returns should be adjusted. 6. Counter-claims for specific performance and holding charges wrongly rejected on limitation grounds. ================================================================================ RESPONDENTS' SUBMISSIONS ================================================================================ 1. Appellant made statements on 11.03.2024 before Executing Court promising payment in seven instalments but failed to pay despite no stay granted. 2. Remaining three co-allottees obtained similar refund awards on identical findings. Appellant selectively challenged only this Award. ================================================================================ FINDINGS AND ANALYSIS ================================================================================ ON SCOPE OF SECTION 34 REVIEW: Post-2015 amendment, scope under Section 34 is "significantly circumscribed". Mere erroneous application of substantive law does not furnish valid grounds unless falling within 'patent illegality' under Section 34(2A) or 'public policy' under Section 34(2)(b)(ii), citing Ssangyong Engineering (2019) 15 SCC 131. ON SECTION 55 DEFENSE: Factual premise underlying Section 55 reliance is absent. Appellant "unilaterally discontinued payment" of assured returns from 01.05.2010, whereas termination occurred on 18.04.2013. Having discontinued payments, Appellant cannot invoke Addendum as defense. Section 54 of Contract Act embodies that party failing to perform its reciprocal promise cannot insist upon performance by other party. ON FORCE MAJEURE: Arbitral Tribunal concluded Appellant was "fully aware" of statutory obligation to obtain ASI NOC before construction. Commencing construction without NOC was impermissible. Entering Agreement on 02.05.2008 with notice of missing NOC disentitled force majeure claim for 2008-2012 period. ASI granted NOC on 27.07.2007 for 15 meters only; attempting 30 meters construction was illegal. ON COUNTER-CLAIMS: Given proper termination and refund order, reliefs for specific performance and holding charges cannot be granted. Counter-claim properly held barred by limitation. ON INTEREST AT 14%: Tribunal considered various Agreement clauses reserving Appellant's right to recover at 18-24% interest. Noting "suppression of material information" and that Respondents were "made to run from pillar to post from 2008 to 2020", Tribunal awarded 14% simple interest from 01.05.2011 to 20.03.2020 and 12% thereafter. Clause 26(f) providing 6% interest has no application as it contemplates delay due to force majeure, which was decided against Appellant. ON NON-JOINDER: Shanmughasundaram v. Diravia Nadar (2005) 10 SCC 278 distinguished. Here, both Respondents were parties to Agreement and arbitration. Award does not affect rights of independent third-party co-owners. ================================================================================ DIRECTIONS AND CONCLUSION ================================================================================ 1. Appellant directed to forthwith deposit awarded amount with up-to-date interest with Executing Court within one week. 2. Amount payable to Respondent No. 2 shall be released immediately. 3. Amount for Respondent No. 1 shall be released only after producing necessary permission from Court dealing with proceedings pursuant to Supreme Court order dated 13.05.2025. 4. Appeal DISMISSED with costs of Rs. 2,00,000/- payable equally to Respondents within two weeks. Proof of payment to be filed within two weeks. 5. Pending applications dismissed. ================================================================================ KEY LEGAL PRINCIPLES ================================================================================ 1. Party failing to perform reciprocal obligations cannot invoke contractual defenses (Section 54, Contract Act). 2. Force majeure defense unavailable when party had notice of impediment before contract execution. 3. Unilateral discontinuation of assured returns constitutes breach precluding reliance on delay clauses. 4. Arbitral awards enjoy limited judicial review under Section

34 - mere legal errors insufficient for interference. 5. Interest rates must be equitable considering parties' conduct and duration of dispute. 6. Non-joinder of co-allottees not fatal where actual parties to agreement seek enforcement of their proportionate rights. ================================================================================ V. KAMESWAR RAO, J. MANMEET PRITAM SINGH ARORA, J. AUGUST 14, 2026 Source: Indian Kanoon (indiankanoon.org/doc/146304896/) Downloaded: October 2026

CASE TITLE: National Insurance Company Limited v. Shafiq-ur-Rehman Nengroo & Ors. COURT: High Court of Jammu and Kashmir at Srinagar CASE NO: CIMA No. 13/2015 and CIMA No. 32/2015 DATE: 18th May, 2015 BENCH: Hon'ble Mr. Justice N. Paul Vasanthakumar, Chief Justice; Hon'ble Mr. Justice Ali Mohammad Magrey, Judge ================================================================================ PARTIES ================================================================================ Appellants: National Insurance Company Limited Respondents: 1. Shafiq-ur-Rehman Nengroo (CIMA 13/2015) 2. Tahmeena Akhter & Ghulam Mohi-u-din Sheikh (CIMA 32/2015) Counsel: - For Appellant: Mr. J. A. Kawoosa, Advocate - For Respondents: Mr. S. M. Ayoub, Advocate ================================================================================ FACTS ================================================================================ 1. Respondents insured their buildings/goods with appellant insurance company 2. September 2014 unprecedented floods in Srinagar caused damage to insured properties 3. Respondents lodged insurance claims on 20.11.2014 and 27.11.2015 - AFTER 81 AND 83 DAYS of loss respectively 4. Insurance policy stipulated claims must be submitted WITHIN 15 DAYS of loss 5. Appellant rejected claims citing delayed submission beyond 15-day period 6. Appellant had extended deadline to 01.10.2014 for flood victims 7. J&K State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission set aside rejection and directed appellant to register and settle claims on merits ================================================================================ LEGAL PROVISIONS CITED ================================================================================ STATUTES: - Insurance Act, 1938 - Sections 2, 2(1A), 2(8), 2(9), 3, 14 - Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority Act, 1999 - Section 3, 14 - Companies Act, 1956 - Indian Partnership Act, 1932 REGULATORY CIRCULARS: - IRDA Circular dated 20.09.2011 - regarding delay in claim intimation/documents submission CASE LAW: - AIR 1966 SC 1644 - United India Insurance Co. Ltd v. Harchand Rai Chandan Lal (2004) 8 SCC 644 - Suraj Mal Ram Niwas Oil Mills Pvt. Ltd v. United India Insurance Co. Ltd. (2010) 10 SCC 567 - National Insurance Company Ltd. v. Alfa Home Appliances, CIMA No. 4/2015 (Division Bench of J&K High Court) ================================================================================ ARGUMENTS ================================================================================ APPELLANT'S CONTENTIONS: 1. Insurance policy explicitly required notice within 15 days of loss 2. Company extended period to 01.10.2014 considering flood situation 3. Claims submitted after more than two months cannot be entertained 4. Commission erred in directing registration without respecting policy conditions RESPONDENTS' CONTENTIONS: 1. Policy itself empowers insurance company to extend time beyond 15 days 2. Unprecedented flood situation constituted sufficient cause for delay 3. "Srinagar City was effected by the fury of floods for more than two months" 4. People had evacuated to safer places and could only return later 5. Delay properly explained and should be condoned 6. Issue covered by Division Bench judgment in CIMA No. 4/2015 ================================================================================ COURT'S REASONING ================================================================================ KEY FINDINGS: 1. POLICY INTERPRETATION: Insurance policy, while stipulating 15 days, gave "ample power...to consider belated claims" and appellant itself exercised this by extending to 01.10.2014 2. GROUND REALITIES: Court noted: "The fact namely the flood has caused heavy damage to the buildings/offices and whole Srinagar City became standstill is beyond doubt" 3. REGULATORY FRAMEWORK: IRDA Circular of 20.09.2011 mandates: "insurers must not repudiate such claims unless and until the reasons of delay are specifically ascertained, recorded" 4. STATISTICAL EVIDENCE: Court referenced its own order

dated 01.10.2014 showing insurance companies had received thousands of claims but settled very few due to flood situation 5. NATURE OF DELAY: Delay was "not willful and due to the peculiar circumstances under which the respondents were put in" 6. PRECEDENT: Division Bench in Alfa Home Appliances case held similar delays should be condoned given unprecedented flood situation 7. LIMITED SCOPE OF ORDER: Commission only directed registration and processing on merits, not automatic allowance of claims ================================================================================ FINAL ORDER ================================================================================ THE HIGH COURT: 1. DISMISSED both appeals 2. UPHELD Commission's order setting aside rejection 3. CONFIRMED direction to appellant to register claims and process them on merits WITHOUT REFERENCE TO DELAY 4. NO COSTS ordered OPERATIVE PORTION: "There is no merit in these appeals and the same are dismissed. No costs." ================================================================================ LEGAL PRINCIPLES ESTABLISHED ================================================================================ 1. TIME LIMITS DIRECTORY: Time limits in insurance policies for claim submission are DIRECTORY, NOT MANDATORY when policy itself contemplates extension 2. REGULATORY COMPLIANCE: Regulatory authority circulars binding on registered insurance companies 3. TECHNICAL GROUNDS INSUFFICIENT: Claims cannot be rejected on TECHNICAL GROUNDS OF DELAY ALONE without examining merits 4. FORCE MAJEURE CIRCUMSTANCES: Natural disasters constitute valid grounds for condonation of delay 5. GROUND REALITIES: Courts must consider GROUND REALITIES while interpreting contractual clauses 6. IRDA DIRECTIVES BINDING: Insurance companies regulated under Insurance Act must comply with IRDA directives 7. DELAY CONDONATION IN DISASTERS: Unprecedented natural disasters warrant liberal approach to time limits for claim submission 8. EXTENSION POWER: Insurance companies having exercised power to extend deadline cannot arbitrarily refuse further reasonable extensions in genuine cases 9. NON-WILLFUL DELAY: Delays not willful but arising from circumstances beyond claimant's control must be condoned 10. LIMITED RELIEF APPROPRIATE: Directing registration and merit-based consideration does not amount to granting claim; preserves insurer's right to reject on substantive grounds ================================================================================ OBSERVATIONS ================================================================================ This judgment is particularly significant for: - DISASTER MANAGEMENT: Establishes precedent for insurance claims following natural disasters - REGULATORY OVERSIGHT: Emphasizes binding nature of IRDA circulars on insurance companies - CONSUMER PROTECTION: Balances contractual terms with equitable considerations - PROCEDURAL FAIRNESS: Distinguishes between procedural delays and substantive merit of claims The Court balanced: - Contractual obligations vs humanitarian considerations - Policy terms vs regulatory mandates - Technical compliance vs substantial justice - Insurer's commercial interests vs public welfare after natural calamity ================================================================================ Judges: (Ali Mohammad Magrey), Judge | (N. Paul Vasanthakumar), Chief Justice Source: Indian Kanoon (indiankanoon.org/doc/101575581/) Downloaded: October 2026

CASE TITLE: Star Health and Allied Insurance Co.Ltd vs A.Chokkar COURT: Madras High Court - Madurai Bench DATE: 26 February, 2010 BENCH: Hon'ble Mrs. Justice Prabha Sridevan and Hon'ble Mr. Justice B. Rajendran CASE NO: Writ Appeal (MD) No.480 of 2009 and connected writ petitions ================================================================================ PARTIES ================================================================================ Appellant/Respondent: Star Health and Allied Insurance Co.Ltd., represented by its Project Officer, Tamil Nadu Government Employees New Health Insurance Scheme Respondent-1/Petitioners: A.Chokkar and others (Government employees/beneficiaries) Respondent-2: The Special Secretary to Government, Finance (Salaries) Department, Government of Tamil Nadu ================================================================================ FACTS ================================================================================ 1. Government of Tamil Nadu implemented new health insurance scheme vide G.O.Ms.No.430, Finance (Salaries) Department, dated 10.09.2007, replacing earlier Tamil Nadu Government Employees Health Fund Scheme. 2. KEY FEATURES OF NEW SCHEME: - Cashless facility - Coverage of Rs.2 lakhs per four-year block period - Mandatory participation with Rs.25/- monthly deduction from salary - Treatment only at network hospitals (375 hospitals initially) - Coverage for specified diseases/procedures listed in Annexure-II 3. In lead case (WA 480/2009), respondent's wife underwent bypass heart surgery at non-network hospital in Thiruvananthapuram. Insurance company rejected claim as hospital was not empanelled. 4. Multiple petitions filed by government employees whose claims were rejected, falling into three categories: - CATEGORY-A: Treatment in non-network hospitals - CATEGORY-B: Procedures/treatments not covered by scheme - CATEGORY-C: Payments made in network hospitals for covered procedures (violating cashless provision) ================================================================================ LEGAL PROVISIONS ================================================================================ 1. G.O.Ms.No.430, Finance (Salaries) Department, dated 10.09.2007 - Introducing new health insurance scheme 2. Tamil Nadu Government Employees New Health Insurance Scheme Rules, 2007 - Defining eligibility, procedures, network hospitals, and grievance redressal mechanism 3. Tamil Nadu Medical Attendance Rules - Pre-existing rules for medical reimbursement claims 4. CONSTITUTIONAL PROVISIONS: - Article 21 - Right to life - Article 47 - State's duty to raise level of nutrition and standard of living - Article 142 - Supreme Court's power to do complete justice - Article 309 - Power to prescribe conditions of service ================================================================================ ARGUMENTS ================================================================================ FOR INSURANCE COMPANY (APPELLANT): - Scheme operates on three strict conditions: (i) cashless facility, (ii) treatment only at network hospitals, (iii) coverage limited to specified procedures - "The insurance policy between the insurer and the insured represents a contract between the parties" - relationship is purely contractual - Insurance company has reinsurance contracts that cover risks only when terms strictly adhered to - Beneficiaries provided Star Medical Insurance Guide clearly specifying network hospitals and covered procedures - Maximum network hospitals established in each district to ensure accessibility - Claims outside scheme terms cannot be settled as it would amount to rewriting contract FOR GOVERNMENT (ADVOCATE GENERAL): - Insurance company cannot be burdened with liabilities outside contract terms - Paragraph 9 of scheme provides grievance redressal mechanism headed by District Collector with medical expert - Tamil Nadu Medical Attendance Rules remain in force and can be invoked for claims not covered by insurance scheme - Employees have alternative remedy under existing rules FOR CLAIMANTS/PETITIONERS: - Scheme participation is mandatory, not optional - Rs.25/- automatically

deducted from salary - Emergency situations may necessitate treatment at non-network hospitals - Beneficiaries may lack choice when specialists refer them to non-network facilities - Network hospitals sometimes demand payment despite cashless provision - Historical precedent: "this Court always directed the Government to reimburse the claim" in pre-scheme cases - Denial of benefits after premium payment is unjust ================================================================================ JUDGMENTS CITED ================================================================================ 1. AIR 1999 SC 3252 - Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Sony Cheriyam: "terms of the agreement have to be strictly construed to determine the extent of liability of the insurer" 2. (2004) 8 SCC 644 - United India Insurance Co. Ltd. vs. Harchand Rai Chandan Lal: Terms of policy govern contract; expressions interpreted per policy definition 3. (2009) 4 MLJ 811 (SC) - Vikram Greentech (I) Ltd. v. New India Assurance Co. Ltd.: "insurance contract, is a species of commercial transactions and must be construed like any other contract" 4. AIR 1996 SC 2426 - P.B.Khet Mazdoor Samity v. State of W.B.: "it is the constitutional obligation of the State to provide adequate medical services to the people" 5. AIR 1996 SC 1051 - Chameli Singh v. State of U.P.: "Right to live guaranteed in any civilised society implies the right to food, water, decent environment, education, medical care" 6. 2008 (5) SCC 328 - State of Karnataka v. R.Vivekananda Swamy: "Rules regarding reimbursement of medical claim...can be made limited" ================================================================================ COURT'S REASONING AND FINDINGS ================================================================================ 1. CONTRACTUAL NATURE: Relationship between insurance company and beneficiaries is purely contractual. Insurance company cannot be compelled to settle claims outside contract terms. 2. DISTINCTION FROM EARLIER CASES: Previous judgments directing reimbursement arose before this scheme, when question was whether denial was arbitrary. "In this case, we are faced with a claim that should be decided against the terms and conditions of the contract." 3. NO POWER TO REWRITE CONTRACT: "if we issue direction to the insurance company to reimburse the claim, we would be virtually re-writing the contract which we are not entitled to" 4. ALTERNATIVE REMEDY AVAILABLE: Tamil Nadu Medical Attendance Rules remain in force, providing remedy for claims not covered by insurance scheme. 5. MANDATORY GUIDELINES NEEDED: Since scheme participation is mandatory with automatic deductions, Government must issue clear guidelines for exceptional situations. ================================================================================ DIRECTIONS ISSUED ================================================================================ Court directed State Government to: 1. CLARIFY ALTERNATIVE REMEDY: Make clear that if claimant cannot take treatment at network hospital for satisfactory reasons, claim can be considered under Tamil Nadu Medical Attendance Rules. 2. UNCOVERED PROCEDURES: If advised procedure not covered by scheme, claimant can apply under the Rules. 3. PREVENT DUPLICATION: Ensure claimants certify they haven't made duplicate claims under both scheme and Rules. 4. HOSPITAL COMPLIANCE: Inform every network hospital that demanding money for admission/treatment will result in removal from network, as this is cashless scheme. 5. NO DENIAL UNDER RULES: Government shall not deny validly made claims under Rules merely because claimant is member of insurance scheme. ================================================================================ FINAL ORDER ================================================================================ 1. WRIT APPEAL NO.480/2009: ALLOWED. Order of

learned Single Judge is SET ASIDE. 2. ALL CONNECTED WRIT PETITIONS: DISPOSED OF with directions that: - Insurance company not liable for claims outside contract terms (non-network hospitals, uncovered procedures, or cash payments) - Petitioners/claimants may approach Government under Tamil Nadu Medical Attendance Rules - Those who have not yet settled claims and require treatment for uncovered procedures may approach Grievance Redressal Committee 3. GRIEVANCE REDRESSAL COMMITTEE: Limited to deciding complaints regarding treatment difficulties, non-availability of facilities, and bogus claims. Cannot direct cash payments as scheme is cashless. 4. No order as to costs. 5. Connected M.Ps. closed. ================================================================================ KEY LEGAL PRINCIPLES ESTABLISHED ================================================================================ 1. Insurance contracts must be strictly construed according to their terms; courts cannot expand coverage beyond contractual obligations. 2. Mandatory participation in government insurance schemes does not eliminate contractual nature of relationship between insurer and insured. 3. When government implements mandatory insurance scheme, alternative remedies under existing rules must remain available for situations not covered by scheme. 4. Government has constitutional obligation to provide medical services, which must be fulfilled through either insurance scheme or alternative mechanisms like Medical Attendance Rules. 5. "Cashless" schemes genuinely require no payments by beneficiaries; violations must be strictly enforced against network hospitals. 6. COURTS CANNOT REWRITE INSURANCE CONTRACTS even when scheme participation is mandatory and beneficiary has paid premiums. 7. Balance between contractual terms and constitutional obligations requires government to maintain parallel remedy mechanism. ================================================================================ Source: Indian Kanoon (indiankanoon.org/doc/1509950/) Downloaded: October 2026

CASE TITLE: Sanjeev Arora vs Ritu Maheshwari, CEO, Greater Noida COURT: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad COURT NO: 7 CASE TYPE: Contempt Application (Civil) No. 366 of 2023 JUDGMENT DATE: 18 April, 2023 BENCH: Hon'ble Justice Rohit Ranjan Agarwal ================================================================================ PARTIES ================================================================================ Applicant: Sanjeev Arora Opposite Party: Ritu Maheshwari, CEO, Greater Noida Counsel for Applicant: Rohan Gupta Counsel for Opposite Party: Anjali Upadhya, Kaushalendra Nath Singh ================================================================================ BACKGROUND FACTS ================================================================================ 1. Applicant was allottee of flat in housing colony developed by Authority 2. Filed application before RERA complaining about delayed possession 3. RERA allowed application on 24.02.2021, directing: - Delivery of possession to petitioner - Payment of interest @ MCLR + 1% - Other directions 4. Non-compliance led to execution proceedings under Section 63 5. Recovery certificate issued on 24.06.2022 6. Writ Petition No. 34081 of 2022 disposed of on 24.11.2022 ================================================================================ PREVIOUS ORDER (24.11.2022) ================================================================================ Writ Court had directed: - Flat was ready for possession - District Magistrate and respondent to ensure recovery/payment within four weeks - Petitioner could approach Authority to take possession ================================================================================ PRESENT PROCEEDINGS ================================================================================ APPLICANT'S CONTENTIONS: - Authority demanded Rs. 5,14,000/- as delayed payment/penalty - Delay attributable to Authority, not applicant - Sought contempt action for non-compliance OPPOSITE PARTY'S RESPONSE: - Authority had deposited penalty with RERA for delayed possession - Ready to handover possession subject to: * Execution of lease deed * Payment of charges by applicant ================================================================================ COURT'S ANALYSIS ================================================================================ The Court observed: 1. "The order of the writ Court was to the extent that either the District Magistrate should recover the amount...or the applicant be given possession" 2. Authority was ready to handover possession upon request 3. "The conditions put down by the applicant that he will not pay the charges...cannot be accepted" 4. Court cannot "dwell into such question of disputed fact" 5. Modification of order dated 24.11.2021 should be sought from Writ Court ================================================================================ FINAL ORDER ================================================================================ The contempt application is DISMISSED. REASONING: - Authority is ready to handover possession - Applicant is ready to take possession but unwilling to pay required charges for lease deed execution - This involves disputed questions of fact - Court declined to interfere - Remedy lies in approaching Writ Court for modification Order Date: 18.04.2023 ================================================================================ KEY LEGAL PRINCIPLES ================================================================================ 1. CONTEMPT JURISDICTION LIMITED: Contempt jurisdiction not appropriate for resolving factual disputes about payment obligations. 2. COMPLIANCE MUST BE COMPLETE: Parties cannot selectively comply with court orders while rejecting associated obligations. 3. CONDITIONAL READINESS: When party expresses readiness to comply subject to counter-performance, contempt may not lie. 4. DISPUTED FACTS: Courts decline to adjudicate disputed factual questions in contempt proceedings. 5. PROPER REMEDY: Modification of original order should be sought from court that passed it, not through contempt proceedings. 6. EXECUTION vs CONTEMPT: Disputed payment obligations better resolved through execution proceedings than contempt. ================================================================================ OBSERVATIONS ================================================================================ This judgment indicates that: - RERA orders for possession must be complied with by both parties - Housing authorities cannot unilaterally impose additional charges without court approval

when RERA has already directed possession - Allottees must also fulfill legitimate payment obligations for lease deed execution - Contempt is not a substitute for proper adjudication of payment disputes - The balance between buyer's rights under RERA and seller's legitimate dues requires careful examination ================================================================================ Source: Indian Kanoon (indiankanoon.org/doc/4658350/) Downloaded: October 2026

DOCUMENT: RERA Authority - Interest Calculation Guidelines SOURCE: Multiple RERA Authority Orders across States APPLICABLE: Section 18 RERA Act, 2016 INTEREST CALCULATION PRINCIPLES: 1. RATE OF INTEREST: As per RERA Rules (State-specific): - Maharashtra: State Bank MCLR + 2% - Karnataka: State Bank MCLR + 2% - UP: State Bank MCLR + 1% - Delhi: State Bank MCLR + 2% - Haryana: State Bank MCLR + 2% Current MCLR (indicative): ~8.85% Typical Interest Rate: 10.85% per annum 2. INTEREST PERIOD: FROM: Due date of possession (as per agreement + grace period) TO: Actual date of possession OR date of refund order 3. CALCULATION METHOD: Simple Interest (not compound) Formula: (Principal × Rate × Time) / 100 Example: Amount Paid: Rs. 50,00,000 Delay: 2 years Rate: 10.85% p.a. Interest = 50,00,000 × 10.85 × 2 / 100 = Rs. 10,85,000 4. GRACE PERIOD CONSIDERATION: - Contractual grace period (typically 6-12 months) allowed - Extended beyond grace = delay period - Force majeure claims rarely accepted - Burden on promoter to prove 5. PARTIAL PAYMENTS: Interest calculated on: - Installments from respective payment dates - Booking amount from booking date - Each payment treated separately 6. REFUND vs POSSESSION: If buyer opts for REFUND: - Return principal + interest - Interest from first payment till refund date If buyer opts to STAY: - Interest till possession date - Continue with allotment 7. TYPICAL RERA ORDERS INCLUDE: a) Direction to pay interest b) Timeline for compliance (usually 90 days) c) Penalty for non-compliance d) Right to execute as decree 8. COMMON PROMOTER DEFENSES (Usually Rejected): - Force majeure (unless proven) - Regulatory delays (unless beyond control) - Buyer payment delays (if not material) - "Tentative timeline" claims (contractual date binds) 9. BUYER OBLIGATIONS: - Paid 10-20% of sale consideration (standing to complain) - Payments as per demand letters - No willful default 10. INTEREST ON DELAYED EMI (If applicable): If buyer delayed EMI payments: - Promoter can claim interest at same rate - Adjusted against interest due to buyer - Must be proved with evidence ENFORCEMENT: Recovery as: - Public dues (some states) - Civil court decree execution - Recovery through District Collector NON-COMPLIANCE PENALTY: - Additional interest @ 1% per month - Prosecution under Section 69 RERA - Imprisonment up to 3 years - Project deregistration APPELLATE REMEDY: - Appeal to Real Estate Appellate Tribunal (30 days) - Further appeal to High Court (60 days) - only on law RECENT TRENDS: - Stricter enforcement - Quick disposal (6 months target) - Online hearings - Consolidated orders for multiple buyers SAMPLE CALCULATION TABLE: Date | Amount | Days | Interest @ 10.85% -----|--------|------|------------------ Booking: Rs. 5L | 1095 days | Rs. 16,289 1st Install: Rs. 10L | 1000 days | Rs. 29,726 2nd Install: Rs. 15L | 800 days | Rs. 35,671 Final: Rs. 20L | 600 days | Rs. 35,671 Total Interest: Rs. 1,17,357 DOCUMENTATION REQUIRED: - Agreement copy - Payment receipts - Demand letters - Correspondence with promoter - Project registration
certificate - Occupancy certificate status Source: Compilation from State RERA Authority Orders Category: RERA Practice & Procedure

SUPREME COURT - CONSUMER PROTECTION ACT PRINCIPLES COMPILATION OF KEY JUDGMENTS SOURCE: Multiple Supreme Court Judgments (1991-2024) CATEGORY: Consumer Law - Legal Principles KEY DEFINITIONS: 1. CONSUMER (Section 2(1)(d)): Person who buys goods/services for consideration for self-use, not for resale or commercial purpose. EXCEPTION: Person using goods/services for livelihood by self-employment IS a consumer. [Laxmi Engineering Works v PSG Industrial Institute (1995)] 2. DEFICIENCY (Section 2(1)(g)): Fault, imperfection, shortcoming in quality, nature, manner of performance required by law or contract. 3. SERVICE (Section 2(1)(o)): Includes service of any description made available to users - excludes personal service under employment contract. LANDMARK PRINCIPLES: A. BURDEN OF PROOF: - Onus on complainant to prove purchase and deficiency - Once prima facie case made, burden shifts to opposite party - Preponderance of probabilities standard (not beyond reasonable doubt) [Spring Meadows Hospital v Harjol Ahluwalia (1998)] B. MEDICAL NEGLIGENCE: - Res Ipsa Loquitur applies (thing speaks for itself) - Bolam test: Doctor not negligent if acted per acceptable practice - Must prove: (i) Duty of care (ii) Breach (iii) Causation (iv) Damages [Jacob Mathew v State of Punjab (2005)] C. HOUSING/CONSTRUCTION DEFICIENCY: - Delayed possession = Deficiency in service - Compensation for mental agony separate from refund - Specific performance or refund - buyer's choice - Builder can't unilaterally change specifications [Lucknow Development Authority v MK Gupta (1994)] D. INSURANCE CLAIMS: - Unreasonable delay in settlement = Deficiency - Repudiation must be bona fide and justified - Contra proferentem rule - construe against insurer - Section 45 protection after 3 years [LIC v Consumer Education Research (1995)] E. BANKING SERVICES: - Banking is "service" under CP Act - Deficiency in cheque clearing, wrong debits, etc. - Harassment for loan recovery = unfair trade practice - Bank liable for negligence of employees [State Bank of India v Shri Rameshwar (2005)] F. UNFAIR TRADE PRACTICE: - False representation - Misleading advertisement - Hoarding/black marketing - Warranty/guarantee defaults [Tata Motors v Surinder Kumar (2012)] G. COMPENSATION: Types of Compensation: i. Refund of price paid ii. Actual financial loss iii. Mental agony (Rs. 10,000 to Rs. 5,00,000 typical) iv. Litigation costs v. Punitive damages (rare cases) Factors for quantum: - Nature of deficiency - Degree of negligence - Financial status of parties - Mental agony suffered - Loss of opportunity [Kishore Lal v Chairman, JAC (2008)] H. MEDICAL NEGLIGENCE COMPENSATION: - Loss of earnings (actual + future) - Medical expenses (past + future) - Attendant charges - Special diet/care - Pain and suffering - Loss of amenities of life - Loss of expectation of life [National Insurance Co. v Pranay Sethi (2017)] I. LIMITATION: - 2 years from cause of action - Cause of action: When deficiency/defect arose OR came to knowledge - Condonable if sufficient cause shown [Secretary, KSRTC v Mrs. Susamma Thomas (1994)] J. VICARIOUS LIABILITY: - Principal liable for agent's acts - Manufacturer liable for dealer's misrepresentation - Employer liable for employee's negligence [Calcutta Medical Research Institute v Bimalesh Chatterjee (2009)] K. PRODUCT LIABILITY (Post

2019 Act): - Strict liability on manufacturer - Defenses: Unavoidable technological limitation, buyer aware of defect - Compensation up to Rs. 1 crore [Sections 82-87, CP Act 2019] L. E-COMMERCE: - E-commerce entity liable if seller info not provided - Platform not vicariously liable if intermediary only - Mandatory grievance officer appointment [Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020] M. SERVICE TAX: Where service tax included in charges: - Consumer entitled to refund if service deficient - Service tax element refundable [Amrit Vanaspati Co. Ltd. v NCDRC (2006)] N. INTEREST: - On refund: 9% per annum typical - From date of payment till realization - On compensation: Court discretion [Kishore Lal case] O. COSTS: - Awarded to successful party - Nominal costs (Rs. 5,000 to Rs. 50,000 typical) - Can be higher for frivolous litigation [Punjab Water Supply v Adarsh Bakshi (2007)] P. APPEAL: District Forum → State Commission → National Commission → Supreme Court (only on law) Deposit required at each stage (50% of awarded amount or as directed) RECENT DEVELOPMENTS: 2019 Act Changes: ✓ Product liability provisions ✓ E-commerce regulations ✓ Mediation as alternate remedy ✓ Pecuniary limits increased (District: Rs. 1 crore, State: Rs. 10 crore) ✓ Central Consumer Protection Authority created COVID-19 IMPACT: - Virtual hearings permitted - Limitation period relaxed - Force majeure claims scrutinized IMPORTANT CASES: 1. Lucknow Development Authority v MK Gupta (1994) - Deficiency in housing 2. Spring Meadows Hospital v Harjol (1998) - Medical negligence standard 3. Jacob Mathew v State (2005) - Bolam test in India 4. Indian Medical Assn v VP Shantha (1995) - Medical service = Service 5. National Insurance v Pranay Sethi (2017) - Accident compensation 6. Nizam's Institute v B Vijay Kumar (2008) - Educational institutions liable 7. M/S National Seeds v M Madhusudhan Reddy (2012) - Farmers as consumers PRACTICE POINTERS: ✓ File within limitation ✓ Proper valuation for jurisdiction ✓ All documents annexed ✓ Specific prayers in complaint ✓ Evidence of payment + deficiency ✓ Legal notice advisable but not mandatory ✓ Consumer can appear in person (no advocate mandatory) Source: Supreme Court Judgments Compilation Category: Consumer Protection Law - Principles

CASE: National Seeds Corporation vs M.Madhusudhan Reddy COURT: Supreme Court of India YEAR: 2012 CITATION: Civil Appeal No. 7543/2004 KEY ISSUE: Whether farmers can claim compensation under Consumer Protection Act for defective seeds FACTS: - Farmers purchased seeds from National Seeds Corporation - Seeds showed poor germination (60% vs expected 90%+) - Uneven plant height (3-6 feet), irregular flowering - Expected yield 600-700 kg/acre, actual 150-200 kg/acre - Claims rejected; farmers approached Consumer Forums NSCL ARGUED: - Seeds Act 1966 is special legislation; Consumer Forums lack jurisdiction - Farmers are not "consumers" - purchased for commercial purpose - Section 13(1)(c) not followed - no laboratory testing of samples - Arbitration clause bars Consumer Forum jurisdiction FARMERS ARGUED: - Seeds Act provides only criminal prosecution, no compensation mechanism - Purchased for livelihood through self-employment - falls within consumer definition - Entire seed quantity used for sowing; sample retention impractical - Expert field inspection by agricultural officers sufficient evidence SUPREME COURT HELD: 1. Consumer Forums have jurisdiction - Seeds Act and Consumer Act operate in different spheres 2. Farmers are "consumers" - seeds purchased for earning livelihood, not resale 3. Section 13(1)(c) strict compliance not mandatory - expecting farmers to retain samples unrealistic 4. Arbitration clause no bar - Consumer Act provides "additional remedy" 5. Expert field inspection sufficient evidence given ground realities PRINCIPLE ESTABLISHED: Farmers entitled to compensation under Consumer Protection Act for defective seeds causing crop failure. Special regulatory legislation does not exclude consumer protection remedies. RESULT: Appeals dismissed. Compensation awards upheld. Costs of Rs. 25,000 per case awarded. Source: Indian Kanoon

CASE: Ebix Singapore vs Committee of Creditors of Educomp COURT: Supreme Court of India YEAR: 2021 BENCH: Justice M.R. Shah & Justice D.Y. Chandrachud KEY ISSUE: Can successful resolution applicant withdraw resolution plan after CoC approval but before NCLT confirmation under IBC? FACTS: Three consolidated appeals: 1. EBIX: Sought withdrawal citing fraud investigations, delays (27 months) 2. KUNDAN CARE: Sought withdrawal citing PPA termination, equipment damage 3. SEROCO: Sought modification reducing payment due to COVID-19 APPLICANTS ARGUED: - Resolution plan not binding until Section 31 NCLT approval - Six-month validity clause expired - Material non-disclosure by Resolution Professional - Changed commercial circumstances - NCLT has inherent powers under Section 60(5) COC ARGUED: - IBC is complete code with no withdrawal provision - Plan becomes binding upon CoC approval - Clause 1.8.4 states plan is "irrevocable" - Withdrawals undermine maximization of value objective - Limited judicial review - cannot second-guess CoC SUPREME COURT HELD: 1. NO UNILATERAL WITHDRAWAL POST-COC APPROVAL "Successful Resolution Applicant does not have right to withdraw after CoC approval" 2. STATUTORY FRAMEWORK GOVERNS "IBC is complete code...no provision permitting withdrawal" 3. LIMITED JUDICIAL REVIEW "NCLT jurisdiction confined to Section 30(2) parameters" 4. VALIDITY CLAUSES RELATE TO SUBMISSION "Six-month validity for keeping offer open for CoC, not withdrawal right" 5. CHANGED CIRCUMSTANCES INSUFFICIENT "Commercial risks assumed; CoC remains decision-maker" 6. NEGOTIATION REMAINS POSSIBLE "May approach CoC for consensual modification; unilateral withdrawal impermissible" PRINCIPLE ESTABLISHED: Resolution plans create binding obligations once CoC approves. No unilateral withdrawal permitted absent statutory provision. Protects creditors, enforces timelines, upholds process sanctity. RESULT: All appeals dismissed. Costs imposed (Rs. 1 crore on Ebix, Rs. 50 lakhs on Kundan). Source: Indian Kanoon

DOCUMENT: Insurance Policy Interpretation - Legal Principles FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES: 1. UTMOST GOOD FAITH (Uberrima Fides) - Insured must disclose all material facts - Section 45 Insurance Act - Incontestability after 3 years 2. CONTRA PROFERENTEM RULE - Ambiguity construed against insurer - Benefit of doubt to insured 3. EXCLUSION CLAUSES - Strictly construed - Burden on insurer to prove CLAIM SETTLEMENT: - Section 64UM Insurance Act - Timeline requirements - IRDA: Claims settled within 30 days - Delayed settlement = deficiency in service LANDMARK JUDGMENTS: 1.
