LIC vs ASHA GOEL (2001) - Burden of proof for non-disclosure on insurer CONSUMER PROTECTION: - Insurance = Service under CP Act - Wrongful repudiation = unfair trade practice - Compensation for mental agony REMEDIES: - Insurance Ombudsman (up to Rs. 1 crore) - Consumer Forums - IRDAI Grievance Cell Source: Compilation from Supreme Court & High Court judgments

CASE TITLE: M/s Spectrum Power Generation Limited vs M/s United India Insurance Company Limited COURT: High Court of Telangana at Hyderabad CASE NO: Commercial Court Appeal No. 26 of 2022 DATE: 2nd January, 2025 BENCH: Hon'ble The Chief Justice Alok Aradhe and Hon'ble Sri Justice J. Sreenivas Rao ================================================================================ PARTIES ================================================================================ Appellant/Plaintiff: M/s Spectrum Power Generation Limited Respondents/Defendants: 1. M/s United India Insurance Company Limited (Lead Insurer) 2. Co-insurer 3. Co-insurer 4. O&M Contractor 5. Original Equipment Manufacturer ================================================================================ BRIEF FACTS ================================================================================ 1. Appellant operates 208 MW combined gas-based power station at Kakinada, Andhra Pradesh. 2. Industrial All Risk (IAR) Policy No. 050100/11/02/059/2002 dated 31.07.2002 for period 01.07.2002 to 30.06.2003, covering material damage and business interruption losses. 3. On 05.11.2002, damage occurred to Steam Turbine Generator (STG) rotor shaft, causing shutdown for approximately 13½ months until 17.12.2003. 4. Plaintiff filed insurance claim for Rs.166,88,71,981/- comprising: - Material damage loss - Business interruption loss for 407 days 5. Insurance company rejected claim vide letters dated 13.05.2005 and 09.11.2005, alleging wilful negligence by O&M contractor's employees. 6. Plaintiff filed suit on 31.05.2008 in O.S.No.451 of 2008, later renumbered as C.O.S.No.134 of 2017. ================================================================================ TRIAL COURT JUDGMENT ================================================================================ Special Court for Commercial Disputes decreed suit IN PART by judgment dated 05.10.2021: ALLOWED: - Material damage claim: Rs.17,79,49,946/- - Interest @ 12% p.a. from 12.05.2003 till realization - Costs: Rs.2,38,15,070/- REJECTED: - Business interruption loss claim for 407 days - Consequential damages ================================================================================ ISSUES BEFORE HIGH COURT ================================================================================ 1. Whether trial court's partial decree is sustainable under law? 2. Whether trial court correctly rejected business interruption loss claim? 3. What relief is plaintiff entitled to? ================================================================================ CONTENTIONS ================================================================================ Appellant's Arguments: 1. "The trial Court without properly appreciating the oral and documentary evidence on record dismissed the suit" for business interruption loss. 2. Interim survey report (Ex.A.12) recommended Rs.24.66 crores for 105 days of business interruption loss. 3. Business interruption loss is "natural/obvious consequence of material damage" under Section II of IAR Policy. 4. Combined cycle plant lost approximately 50% electricity production capacity due to STG shutdown. 5. Defendants filed no appeal against material damage decree, which has become final. Respondents' Arguments: 1. Plaintiff failed to make adequate pleadings regarding business interruption loss. 2. No evidence adduced to prove actual business interruption loss for 407 days. 3. Interim survey report (Ex.A.12) is "not conclusive proof" and lacks details on business interruption. 4. "The plaintiff has not filed any income tax statement" or profit-loss statements to establish loss. 5. Documents Ex.A.35 and Ex.A.36 are unsigned calculation tables without supporting documentation. ================================================================================ LEGAL PROVISIONS CONSIDERED ================================================================================ - Section 13 of the Commercial Courts Act, 2015 - Section 64 UM(2) of the Insurance Act - IAR Policy Sections I (Material Damage) and II (Business Interruption) ================================================================================ ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS ================================================================================ ON BUSINESS INTERRUPTION LOSS: 1. BURDEN OF PROOF: Court held that "mere claiming material damage loss does not entitle the plaintiff to claim the loss due to business interruption." 2. INTERIM SURVEY REPORT: Trial court correctly found Ex.A.12

to be non-conclusive: "in the absence of any final survey report, the same cannot be taken into consideration." 3. LACK OF DOCUMENTARY EVIDENCE: Plaintiff failed to produce: - Income tax returns - Profit and loss statements - Audit reports - Evidence of demand from APTRANSCO - Proof of failure to supply electricity 4. DEFECTIVE CLAIMS DOCUMENTS: Ex.A.35 and Ex.A.36 were "unsigned calculation tables" without supporting documentation, and "there is no indication...as to whether the amount mentioned is in 'Rupees' or 'Lakhs' or 'Crores'." 5. NO FINAL SURVEY: Plaintiff "has not taken any steps prior to institution of suit or subsequent to filing of suit for conducting survey." LEGAL PRINCIPLES APPLIED: Court distinguished cases cited by appellant, noting those involved timely notification and adequate evidence. Court affirmed that while surveyor reports have statutory recognition, they are "not sacrosanct and can be contested by other evidence." ================================================================================ FINAL ORDER ================================================================================ High Court DISMISSED the appeal with following observations: 1. Trial court correctly decreed suit for material damage of Rs.17,79,49,946/- with interest and costs. 2. Rejection of business interruption loss claim was justified due to: - Lack of adequate pleadings - Absence of documentary evidence - Non-conclusive interim survey report - Failure to conduct final survey 3. Trial court's findings based on "cogent findings in respect of each issue" after analyzing oral and documentary evidence. NO ORDER AS TO COSTS. All pending miscellaneous applications stand closed. ================================================================================ KEY LEGAL PRINCIPLES ESTABLISHED ================================================================================ 1. BURDEN OF PROOF IN BUSINESS INTERRUPTION: Claimant must provide comprehensive documentary evidence including tax returns, P&L statements, and audit reports to prove business interruption loss. 2. SURVEYOR REPORTS: Interim survey reports are not conclusive evidence; final survey reports required for substantiating claims. 3. PLEADING REQUIREMENTS: Adequate pleadings specifically detailing business interruption loss are mandatory prerequisite. 4. DOCUMENTARY EVIDENCE: Unsigned calculation tables without supporting documentation have no evidentiary value. 5. MATERIAL DAMAGE vs BUSINESS INTERRUPTION: Proving material damage does not automatically entitle claimant to business interruption compensation - separate proof required. 6. COMPLETENESS OF CLAIMS: Failure to complete insurance survey formalities (conducting final survey) weakens claim substantially. ================================================================================ Alok Aradhe, Chief Justice J. Sreenivas Rao, Judge Date: 2nd January, 2025 Source: Indian Kanoon (indiankanoon.org/doc/62381705/) Downloaded: October 2026

CASE: Vijay Prakash vs UOI (Privacy and RTI) COURT: Delhi High Court YEAR: 2009 CITATION: AIR 2010 DELHI 7 JUDGE: Justice S. Ravindra Bhat KEY ISSUE: Whether public servant's personal information protected under RTI Act Section 8(1)(j) FACTS: - Former IAF officer sought wife's (DRDO employee) service records under RTI - Wife posted at 4 AFSB Varanasi; matrimonial dispute pending - Requested leave forms, DSOP nominations, investment records - Information denied citing Section 8(1)(j) - personal information exemption LEGAL PROVISIONS: Section 8(1)(j) RTI Act: Exempts personal information unless public interest requires disclosure Section 11: Third party information protection COURT HELD: 1. Privacy is fundamental right - cannot be forfeited by becoming public servant 2. Public servants entitled to privacy for personal information unrelated to official duties 3. "Public interest" cannot be presumed merely because subject is government employee 4. Burden on information seeker to establish public interest 5. Matrimonial litigation is private matter - no public interest element PRINCIPLE ESTABLISHED: Personal information of public servants protected unless specific public interest demonstrated regarding accountability/performance of official duties. RESULT: Writ petition dismissed. RTI request properly rejected. Source: Indian Kanoon

CASE: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) vs Union of India COURT: Supreme Court of India (9-Judge Bench) YEAR: 2017 CITATION: (2017) 10 SCC 1 LANDMARK DECISION: RIGHT TO PRIVACY AS FUNDAMENTAL RIGHT HELD: RIGHT TO PRIVACY IS FUNDAMENTAL RIGHT (9-0 Unanimous) "The right to privacy is protected as an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21 and as a part of the freedoms guaranteed by Part III of the Constitution." CONSTITUTIONAL BASIS: - Article 21 - Right to Life and Personal Liberty - Article 14 - Right to Equality - Article 19 - Fundamental Freedoms DIMENSIONS OF PRIVACY: 1. Bodily Privacy - Physical integrity 2. Informational Privacy - Control over personal data 3. Decisional Privacy - Autonomous choices 4. Proprietary Privacy - Identity control THREE-FOLD TEST FOR PRIVACY RESTRICTION: i. Must be through valid law ii. Legitimate state aim iii. Proportionality to objective SIGNIFICANCE: Most important fundamental rights judgment. Foundation for Data Protection Act 2023. Cited in 400+ subsequent cases. Basis for digital age privacy protection. Source: Supreme Court of India | indiankanoon.org/doc/91938676/

CASE TITLE: U.P. Avas Evam Vikas Parishad, Lucknow vs. Dhruv Kumar Chaturvedi and Others COURT: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad, Lucknow Bench BENCH: Hon'ble Justice Om Prakash Shukla DATE OF JUDGMENT: 18 November, 2023 NEUTRAL CITATION: 2023:AHC-LKO:76514 CASE NUMBERS: RERA Appeal Nos. 67-117 of 2023 (51 connected appeals) ================================================================================ PARTIES ================================================================================ Appellant: U.P. Avas Evam Vikas Parishad, Lucknow Respondents: Various allottees including Dhruv Kumar Chaturvedi, Arun Kumar Dwivedi, Pramod Kumar, and 48 others ================================================================================ FACTUAL BACKGROUND ================================================================================ 1. Project Details: The appellant launched Vrindavan Yojna, Nilgiri Enclave housing scheme in March 2013 for 640 flats under self-finance arrangement. 2. Allotments: Various respondents were allotted flats between 2013-2014 with estimated sale considerations and proposed possession timeline of 24-30 months. 3. Delays: Possession was significantly delayed, with flats delivered between 2017-2018, causing delays of 18-24 months beyond stipulated periods. 4. Complaints Filed: Allottees filed complaints before RERA Authority seeking compensation for delayed possession, structural deficiencies, and other issues. 5. Authority Orders: Adjudicating Officer awarded compensation as interest at MCLR+1% for delay periods. 6. Appellate Tribunal: Dismissed appeals filed by Parishad vide common order dated 25.11.2022. ================================================================================ ISSUES RAISED ================================================================================ The appellant framed six "substantial questions of law": (a) Whether impugned order suffers from illegality due to improper consideration and jurisdictional error (b) Whether complaints were maintainable given filing before RERA Act came into force (c) Whether compensation ignoring force majeure circumstances was justified (d) Whether compensation could be awarded under Sections 12, 14 & 18 after complaint dismissal (e) Whether deciding multiple appeals by common order violated natural justice (f) Whether interest award contradicts Supreme Court law ================================================================================ LEGAL PROVISIONS EXAMINED ================================================================================ RERA Act, 2016: - Section 2(q): Definition of "completion certificate" - Section 2(zf): Definition of "occupancy certificate" - Section 2(zn): Definition of "real estate project" - Section 3: Applicability to ongoing projects - Section 12: Obligations of promoters - Section 14: Adherence to sanctioned plans - Section 18(1): Remedies for delayed possession - "If the promoter fails to complete...he shall be liable...to return the amount...with interest" - Section 44: Appeals to Appellate Tribunal - Section 58: Appeals to High Court on substantial questions of law per Section 100 CPC - Section 71: Adjudicating Officer's jurisdiction for compensation - Section 72: Factors for determining compensation ================================================================================ KEY LEGAL PRINCIPLES ESTABLISHED ================================================================================ 1. ONGOING PROJECT STATUS: Applying M/s. Newtech Promoters vs. State of UP (Civil Appeal 6745-6749/2021), Court held: - Act applies to projects where completion certificate not issued before commencement - Completion certificate issued 20.12.2018, post-RERA enactment - Project clearly "ongoing" under Rule 2(h) 2. JURISDICTION OF ADJUDICATING OFFICER: Per Neelkamal Realtors vs. Union of India AIR 2018 (NOC) 398 (Bom): "interest is compensatory in nature...not unreasonable" Court distinguished Newtech case (para 86), holding Adjudicating Officer empowered to award "compensation in form of interest" under Sections 71-72. 3. FORCE MAJEURE: Court upheld Tribunal's finding that farmer agitation didn't constitute "Act of God" or vis major under Section 6 explanation. 4. CONTRACTUAL TERMS vs. STATUTORY RIGHTS: Following Newtech Promoters: "contractual terms

do not have overriding effect over provisions of the Act" Tentative timelines held not to exempt promoter from statutory obligations. 5. POST-POSSESSION RIGHTS: Citing Wg. Cdr. Arifur Rahman Khan vs. DLF Southern Homes (2020) SCC Online 667: Home buyer doesn't lose compensation rights after taking possession. ================================================================================ PRECEDENTS RELIED UPON ================================================================================ 1. M/s. Newtech Promoters and Developers Pvt. Ltd. vs. State of UP (2021) - RERA applicability to ongoing projects 2. Santosh Hazari vs. Purushottam Tiwari (2001) 3 SCC 179 - Substantial question of law test 3. Nazir Mohamed vs. J. Kamala (2020) 19 SCC 57 - Principles under Section 100 CPC 4. Fortune Infrastructure vs. Trevor D'lima (2018) 5 SCC 442 - Indefinite waiting impermissible 5. Pioneer Urban Land vs. Govindan Raghavan II (2019) CPJ 34(SC) - Reasonable interest rates ================================================================================ FINAL ORDER ================================================================================ All 51 appeals dismissed. Key Holdings: 1. No substantial questions of law arose warranting interference 2. Appellate Tribunal correctly applied RERA provisions 3. Projects were "ongoing" under statutory definition 4. Adjudicating Officer had jurisdiction to award compensation as interest 5. Delays attributable to promoter, not force majeure 6. Statutory rights survive execution of sale deed 7. MCLR+1% interest rate fair and reasonable 8. Common disposal of similar appeals proper ================================================================================ CONCLUSION ================================================================================ The Court comprehensively upheld RERA's consumer-protective framework, rejecting technical objections by the housing authority. The judgment reinforces that: - Statutory remedies override contractual limitations - Ongoing projects fall under RERA regardless of allotment dates - Compensation rights continue post-possession - Public authorities bound equally by consumer protection laws Status: Appeals dismissed with no costs ordered. Source: Indian Kanoon (indiankanoon.org/doc/92131005/) Downloaded: October 2026

CASE TITLE: Apex Buildwell Pvt. Ltd. vs Sachin Kumar and Others COURT: High Court of Punjab and Haryana at Chandigarh CASE NO: RERA-APPL-58-2021 (O&M) and connected cases DATE: 26th April, 2022 BENCH: Hon'ble Mr. Justice Anil Kshetarpal ================================================================================ PARTIES ================================================================================ Appellant: Apex Buildwell Pvt. Ltd. Respondents: Sachin Kumar, Poonam Yadav, Varun Munjal, Suman Devi, Akash Mathur, Pardeep Kumar, Madhu Tripathi, Sandeep Grover, Ravin Narain Vats, Nishi Kapoor, Anita Yadav, Krishan Kumar Sachdeva (in various connected appeals) Counsel for Appellant: Mr. Akshay Bhan, Sr. Advocate with Mr. Alok Mittal, Mr. Rohan Gupta, Mr. Arun Gupta Counsel for Respondents: Mr. Gaurav Bhardwaj, Ms. Ayushi Sharma, Mr. Mayank Gupta ================================================================================ FACTS ================================================================================ 1. Appellant-promoter granted licence on 22.02.2012 for "Affordable Housing Project" named 'Our Home', Sector 37, Gurugram, valid until 21.02.2016. 2. Respondent-allottee allotted apartment No.343, 3rd Floor, Tower-Orchid with carpet area of 48 sq. mts. at Rs.16,00,000/-, having paid Rs.15,20,000/-. 3. Apartment Buyer's Agreement (ABA) executed on 12.07.2013, stipulating possession delivery within 36 months plus 6 months grace period. 4. Licence expired on 21.02.2016. Appellant's renewal application received on 14.03.2016. 5. Appellant failed to: - Deposit External Development Charges (EDC) of Rs.1,951.28 lakhs - Renew bank guarantee - Pay complete renewal fee - Remove various deficiencies despite multiple show cause notices (20.06.2017, 14.07.2017, 24.08.2017, 04.10.2016, 22.10.2018, 30.11.2018) 6. Licence ultimately renewed only on 01.04.2019 after appellant deposited Rs.2 Crore renewal fee and complied with requirements on 28.12.2018. 7. Project registered under RERA as ongoing project after Act came into force. ================================================================================ CONTENTIOUS CLAUSES IN ABA ================================================================================ Clause 7(ii)(a) - Interest on Allottee's Default: 18% per annum for first 60 days, then 24% per annum thereafter. Clause 3(c)(iv) - Compensation to Allottee: Rs.10/- per square feet per month on carpet area (approximately 0.37% per annum). COURT'S OBSERVATION: "on the one hand...the flat buyer was liable to pay...18%...24%...on the other hand...0.37% per annum, approximately. The aforesaid term is not only one sided but also unfair and unreasonable." ================================================================================ LEGAL PROVISIONS EXAMINED ================================================================================ Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016: Section 18 - Return of amount and compensation: "If the promoter fails to complete or is unable to give possession...in accordance with the terms of the agreement...he shall be liable...the allottee shall be paid, by the promoter, interest for every month of delay, till the handing over of the possession." Section 2(za) - Interest: "the rate of interest chargeable from the allottee by the promoter, in case of default, shall be equal to the rate of interest which the promoter shall be liable to pay." Section 58 - Appeal to High Court: Appeals maintainable only on substantial questions of law as per Section 100 CPC. Haryana Real Estate Rules, 2017: Rule 15: Interest rate prescribed as "State Bank of India highest marginal cost of lending rate plus two percent." Indian Contract Act, 1872: Section 23: Contracts opposed to public policy are void. Section 32: Contingent contracts on uncertain future events. Section 56: Agreements becoming impossible or unlawful after contract formation. ================================================================================ ISSUES FRAMED ================================================================================ 1.

Whether delay in project completion can be attributed to promoter when licence renewal delayed for over three years. 2. Whether authorities wrongly ignored contractual interest rate on delayed possession. ================================================================================ ARGUMENTS ================================================================================ Appellant's Submissions: 1. Delay in licence renewal (3+ years) beyond promoter's control - Force Majeure. 2. Contractual interest rate (Rs.10/sq.ft/month) should apply, not prescribed statutory rate. 3. RERA registration with extended time should apply to pre-Act agreements. 4. RERA Act should not apply retroactively to existing agreements. Respondents' Position: 1. Delay attributable to appellant's negligence and willful default. 2. Unconscionable contract terms should be ignored as against public policy. 3. RERA provisions apply to ongoing projects retroactively. ================================================================================ COURT'S ANALYSIS ================================================================================ ON FORCE MAJEURE AND DELAY: Court rejected Force Majeure defense: 1. SECTIONS 32 & 56 OF CONTRACT ACT NOT APPLICABLE: "the appellant has failed to bring its case within the four corners of Section 32...From the beginning, the appellant knew that his licence is going to expire in February, 2016." 2. WILLFUL DEFAULT ESTABLISHED: "the appellant has not only been thoroughly negligent but has also committed willful default...failed to take any justifiable steps." 3. CONSTRUCTION NEVER STOPPED: "there is a finding by the Authority-HRERA that the appellant continued with the construction." 4. NO EXCLUSION OF RENEWAL PERIOD: Promoter cannot claim exclusion of period "where delay is wholly or partially attributable to him." ON INTEREST RATE: Court held contractual interest terms VOID: 1. UNCONSCIONABLE TERMS: Cited Section 23, Contract Act - terms opposed to public policy are void. 2. UNEQUAL BARGAINING POWER: "The promoter and the flat buyer do not negotiate on same platform and also do not have equal bargaining power." 3. SUPREME COURT PRECEDENTS APPLIED: - Pioneer Urban Land v. Govindan Raghavan (2019): Dominant unfair terms to be ignored - NBCC v. Shri Ram Trivedi (2021): Unreasonable interest constitutes unfair trade practice - IREO Grace Realtech v. Abhishek Khanna (2021): Court not bound by one-sided contract terms ON RETROACTIVE APPLICATION: Relying on Newtech Promoters v. State of UP (2021): "the provisions of the Act are retroactive...applicable to the projects pending on the date of enforcement." Citing Imperia Structures v. Anil Patni (2020): "extension granted by the authorities to complete the project does not absolve the promoter from its liability to pay interest." ================================================================================ FINDINGS ================================================================================ 1. Delay in licence renewal entirely attributable to appellant's failure to comply with statutory requirements. 2. Contractual interest clause (0.37% p.a. vs 18-24% on allottee's default) is unconscionable, one-sided, and against public policy. 3. RERA provisions apply retroactively to ongoing projects and pre-Act agreements. 4. Prescribed interest rate under Rule 15 (SBI MCLR + 2%) is valid and applicable. 5. Extension of project completion time does not affect allottee's entitlement to interest for delayed possession. ================================================================================ FINAL ORDER ================================================================================ 1. APPEALS DISMISSED: All connected appeals filed by Apex Buildwell Pvt. Ltd. are dismissed. 2. INTEREST AFFIRMED: Orders of HRERA and Appellate Tribunal awarding interest at 10.75% per annum (SBI MCLR + 2%) from 02.06.2017 till date of possession offer are upheld.

3. PENDING APPLICATIONS DISPOSED: All miscellaneous applications stand disposed of. Date: 26th April, 2022 Judge: (Anil Kshetarpal) ================================================================================ KEY LEGAL PRINCIPLES ESTABLISHED ================================================================================ 1. Force Majeure cannot be invoked when delay attributable to party's own negligence and non-compliance. 2. Grossly disproportionate interest clauses in builder-buyer agreements are VOID as against public policy. 3. Courts can ignore unconscionable contractual terms where parties have unequal bargaining power. 4. RERA provisions apply retroactively to ongoing projects irrespective of when agreements executed. 5. Extension of project completion date by authorities does not extinguish allottee's right to compensation for delayed possession. 6. Contractual terms providing 18-24% interest on buyer's default vs 0.37% on builder's default are manifestly unfair and unenforceable. ================================================================================ Source: Indian Kanoon (indiankanoon.org/doc/137910750/) Downloaded: October 2026

LANGUAGE: Use simple, clear language. Avoid legal jargon unless necessary. 2. FACTS: State facts chronologically and clearly. Each paragraph should contain one main fact. 3. PERSONAL KNOWLEDGE: Only state facts within your personal knowledge. For facts learned from others, mention source. 4. TRUTH: All statements must be true. False affidavit = perjury (IPC Section 191). 5. ANNEXURES: If attaching documents, refer to them as: "A copy of [document name] is annexed hereto and marked as Annexure-A" 6. AMENDMENTS: Any corrections should be initialed. No overwriting. 7. SIGNATURE: Sign on each page if multiple pages. Last page must have full signature. 8. NOTARIZATION: Get it notarized or affirmed before Oath Commissioner. 9. STAMP PAPER: Use appropriate value stamp paper as per state laws (typically Rs. 10-100). 10. DATE: Always mention correct date of execution. COMMON USES: ✓ Court proceedings (civil/criminal) ✓ Government applications (passport, visa) ✓ Educational purposes (name correction, certificates) ✓ Banking/financial transactions ✓ Property matters ✓ Employment verification ✓ Immigration purposes ✓ Insurance claims ✓ Change of name/address ✓ Succession/legal heir certificate SAMPLE SPECIFIC AFFIDAVITS CAN BE CREATED FOR: - Name correction - Date of birth proof - Address proof - Income affidavit - Identity affidavit - No objection affidavit - Ownership affidavit - Heirship affidavit
